service-a-la-francaise-to-service-a-la-r.context_blurb:
How a dinner reaches the table has changed as much as what is on it. At a grand French dinner of the 1700s every dish of a course appeared at once in a glittering spread; in the 1800s a Russian style took over in which food came out course by course, and it shaped the way formal dinners are still served today.

In the old style, service à la française, every dish of a course arrived together, and each diner helped himself only from the platters he could physically reach, so his seat decided his dinner, and whatever sat far down the table he never tasted. The spread was a show: dozens of tureens, platters and roasts were laid out in a perfect mirror-image pattern, with towering centrepieces and ornate silver, so the meal was as much a display of abundance as a dinner.

Midway through, servants performed the remove, in French the relève: they carried off a finished dish, classically a great spit-roasted joint in sauce, and set a fresh one down in exactly the same place, so the symmetrical display never looked thinned out or emptied.

Around 1810 the Russian ambassador to France, Prince Alexander Kurakin, set Paris talking with dinners at his residence at Clichy where the dishes came out in turn, one course at a time, instead of spread over the table: the first dinners à la russe. A well-loved story explains the change: on 1 July 1810, at a ball for Napoleon's marriage to Marie-Louise, fire tore through the hall, and Kurakin was trampled and badly burned, bedridden for months and unable to reach across a table, so he had his food brought to him plated, course by course. Historians treat that link as legend, since the Russian habit of serving in sequence existed before him.

Service à la russe fixed the old style's great fault, dishes that sat out for the whole meal and went cold: now each dish came out only when its course arrived, carved in the kitchen or at the sideboard, so hot food arrived hot and meals came in courses.

The new style also put a new object beside the plate. Once the whole feast was no longer laid out for the eye to see, diners could not tell what was coming, so they needed a printed menu card listing the dishes still to come, in the order they would arrive.

sharpening-vs-honing-grinding-a-new-edge.context_blurb:
A chef's knife that seems blunt after days of chopping onions usually is not worn out at all. Keeping a blade keen takes two different jobs that many cooks confuse: honing on a steel rod, done often and in seconds, and sharpening on a stone, done every month or two. Knowing which is which keeps both the knife and the cook's fingers safe.

The honing steel does not sharpen. Everyday cutting rolls the ultra-thin edge over to one side, and a few strokes along the steel simply bend that folded edge back upright into a straight line, removing almost no metal, which is why honing takes seconds and chefs do it constantly.

Real sharpening happens on a whetstone, a flat stone used wet, which actually grinds a tiny sliver of metal off the blade to form a brand-new edge; because it takes metal away, cooks sharpen only every month or two and hone in between. Honing must stay light: the steel's fine grooves catch the rolled edge and nudge it back into line, and four to six gentle strokes on each side are plenty, but bearing down hard can chip tiny flakes out of the fragile edge instead of straightening it.

Honing works only while there is a rolled edge to straighten. Once the edge itself has worn away, there is nothing left to bend back, so steeling stops helping, and that is the sign the knife finally needs the stone. Whetstones are numbered like sandpaper: a low grit such as 400 has big, coarse particles that cut metal fast to set or repair an edge, and a high grit such as 6000 has fine particles that polish it, so a cook starts on the coarse 400 and finishes on the fine 6000. Many stones are two-sided, coarse on one face and fine on the other.

As a sharpener grinds one side of the edge on the stone, the steel there grows so thin that it bends over instead of wearing away cleanly, and a tiny wire lip, the burr, folds onto the far side, the face that is not touching the stone. Finding the burr is the moment a sharpener hopes for, because it appears only once the two ground faces have thinned all the way down and met at the edge. The sharpener checks by drawing a thumb across the edge until the wire catches, then flips the knife and raises a burr on the other side.

The burr is a trap for beginners: it is razor-thin but so weak that it folds flat under the lightest pressure, so a freshly burred knife feels sharp but does not cut like one, and the last job of sharpening is to remove the burr with light, alternating strokes. The final polish is stropping on a strip of leather, which clears away the final scrap of burr and the fine scratches the stone left, and the blade always travels backward, spine first with the edge trailing, because an edge pulled forward would slice into the leather and ruin both strop and blade.

simmer-vs-rolling-boil-gentle-vs-violent.context_blurb:
Recipes keep telling cooks to simmer, boil or poach, and the words are not interchangeable. Water at sea level cannot get hotter than boiling, so the difference among them is how hard the water moves, and some foods need calm water while others need fury.

A simmer shows only a few small bubbles drifting up and now and then breaking an almost still surface, while a rolling boil heaves with large, fast bubbles from edge to edge and pours off steam; cooks judge by the bubbles, not a thermometer.

Turning the burner up does not make boiling water hotter: once water reaches its boiling point it cannot climb any higher, so at sea level a gentle boil and a violent rolling boil both sit at about 212°F, or 100°C, and the rolling boil is simply more agitation. In the thinner air of the mountains the boiling point is lower.

So where does the extra flame go? It goes into tearing liquid water apart into steam, about 540 calories for every gram, which is why a hard boil throws off clouds of steam and boils the pot dry fast while giving the food the same heat as a gentle one, never cooking a potato's middle any quicker.

Pasta is the exception that wants the fury: the strands shed sticky starch as they cook and glue together most in the first minute, so a hard, rolling boil keeps them tumbling apart instead of cementing into one lump. Delicate food is the opposite, because a rolling boil would batter an egg or a fish fillet to shreds.

The gentlest method of all is poaching, at roughly 160 to 180°F, cooler than a simmer: the water barely quivers and no true bubbles break its surface, a state French cooks call frissonner, and it is kept for fragile foods such as eggs, fish and chicken. A poached egg likes about 180 to 190°F, enough to set the white and leave the yolk runny.

sliced-bread-and-the-wrapped-loaf.context_blurb:
Few foods are as ordinary as a loaf of sliced bread, yet its invention took one stubborn jeweller sixteen years and survived a fire, a doubtful baking trade and a wartime ban. Its story runs through the American Midwest and reaches its payoff in a small Missouri town in 1928.

The food we measure great ideas against is sliced bread, and the first business anywhere to sell machine-sliced loaves was the Chillicothe Baking Company of Chillicothe, Missouri, in July 1928. The famous phrase came later, catching on in the 1950s; the comedian Red Skelton used it about television in 1952.

The inventor, Otto Rohwedder, had owned jewellery stores in St. Joseph, Missouri, and spent about sixteen years on his slicer, but in November 1917 a fire at a factory in Monmouth, Illinois, destroyed his prototype and all his blueprints, and he had to start again from scratch.

Bakers doubted him for a good reason: a loaf cut all the way through loses the unbroken crust that holds it together, so it goes stale and falls apart quickly. Rohwedder's answer was a machine that also sealed every freshly cut loaf in a wrapper of wax paper the instant it was sliced, locking in the freshness.

The first loaf went out the door on July 7, 1928, which happened to be Rohwedder's own 48th birthday, and Chillicothe still celebrates the date as Sliced Bread Day.

During World War II, on January 18, 1943, Agriculture Secretary Claude Wickard ordered stores to stop selling sliced bread, to save wax paper and steel. Home cooks raised a furious outcry, joined by New York's mayor Fiorello La Guardia and a congressman who called the ban a dictatorial abuse of power, and it was scrapped by March 8.

smell-is-flavor-retronasal-olfaction.context_blurb:
Chew a cherry jelly bean with your nostrils squeezed closed and it tastes merely sweet; release them and the cherry comes rushing back. That small trick shows that most of what we call taste really happens in the nose, which smells food from inside the mouth by a back route, and scientists have traced how the brain builds flavour out of both senses.

The tongue on its own detects just five basic tastes, sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury umami, and nothing more; cherry and every other particular flavour come from the nose, rising from inside the mouth the moment you let go. That is why a heavy cold makes a favourite dinner taste like cardboard: the taste buds still fire, but a clogged nose cannot pick up the food's aromas, a temporary loss of smell that doctors call anosmia.

Blindfolded, with the nose pinched, a bite of raw apple and a bite of raw potato taste almost the same, because pure taste can report only sweet and crunchy; telling an apple from a potato, a pear or even an onion takes the sense of smell.

Gordon Shepherd, a neuroscientist at Yale, gave a new science the name neurogastronomy, and in his 2012 book he argued that flavour comes mostly from smell and is built in the brain, not on the tongue. Temperature matters too, because warmth makes aroma molecules more volatile, so they rise to the nose in far greater numbers, and a reheated bowl of soup tastes rich while the same soup cold from the fridge seems flat.

Long before brain scanners, the French lawyer and food writer Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin argued in The Physiology of Taste, published in 1825, that taste and smell form one sense, in which the mouth is the laboratory and the nose is the chimney, with aromas rising up like smoke. Shepherd describes the airway as a pump that carries food aromas from the mouth up into the back of the nose, but only when you breathe out; on the in-breath that flow almost stops. The psychologist Paul Rozin summed it up: sniffing the world is breathing in, but tasting food is breathing out.

Warmth changes plain taste as well: a heat-activated channel in the taste buds called TRPM5 makes sweetness come through far more strongly as food warms from about 15 to 35°C, and mice bred without it got no boost. That is why warm, flat cola tastes cloying and why ice cream is sweetened heavily so it still tastes right when frozen.

The brain even sorts smells by where they come from. In 2005 Dana Small's team showed that the same chocolate odour sets off different brain responses when it arrives through the nostrils and when it rises from the back of the mouth.

smoke-cure-and-the-pink-that-means-safe.context_blurb:
Smoking and curing are two of the oldest ways to keep meat without a fridge, and they explain why bacon, ham and hot dogs stay pink when a roast turns grey. Smoke, salt and a mineral that cooks used for centuries without understanding it all fight spoilage, each by a different route, and one deadly germ is the reason the rules matter.

On old farms, pork and fish hung in a smokehouse above a bed of wood chips kept smouldering, never flaming, and the smoke drifting up kept the meat from spoiling and gave bacon and smoked fish their flavour.

Deli smoked salmon is cold-smoked, hung in smoke kept no warmer than about 37°C (99°F), and often much cooler, far below cooking heat, so after hours in the smoker it stays silky and translucent, nearly raw. Smoke barely gets past the surface of a thick ham, so cooks pair it with salt-curing, rubbing the meat thickly with salt, which works its way deep into the core that smoke cannot reach; that is why bacon and country hams are both salted and smoked.

Smoke preserves in two ways at once: the phenol compounds it leaves behind slow bacteria, and they are also antioxidants that shield the meat's fat from slowly turning rancid, while the heat dries the surface into a protective skin. Each wood carries its own flavour compounds locked inside it, and they ride up in the smoke, so hickory, mesquite and applewood barbecue taste different; guaiacol gives the main smoky smell, while vanillin adds sweeter, vanilla-like notes.

A grilled pork chop turns grey-brown, but a hot dog stays pink right through because its meat has been cured. Nitrite in the cure breaks down into nitric oxide, which locks onto the iron in myoglobin, the meat's red pigment, and the new pigment stays pink even after cooking, as it does in ham and bacon.

The main reason for curing salts is botulism, the most dangerous of all food poisons. Its germ, Clostridium botulinum, is an anaerobe that grows only in an airless place, without oxygen, which is why sealed, low-oxygen cured meat is exactly where it could thrive.

For centuries cooks found that saltpeter, potassium nitrate, mixed with salt kept cured meat safer than salt alone and turned it pink, though nobody knew why; we now know saltpeter breaks down into the nitrite that does the work, and the United States formally adopted nitrite and nitrate curing salts in 1925. Today's pink curing salt, sold under names such as Prague Powder #1, is about 94 percent ordinary salt and 6 percent sodium nitrite, which is white on its own, and makers dye it pink on purpose so that no cook ever grabs it instead of table salt, since nitrite is toxic in quantity.

Prosciutto breaks the rule: a hind leg of pork, salted with sea salt and left hanging for between nine months and three years, never meets nitrite, smoke or heat. Salt and time alone make it safe, because over the long months of salting and air-drying the ham loses so much moisture that bacteria can no longer grow in it. Prosciutto di Parma, which may contain only pork legs, sea salt and lard, has been made without nitrite since 1993 with no recorded case of botulism.

smoke-flavor-and-preservation.context_blurb:
For centuries, hams, bacon and fish hung in smokehouses, kept by smoke as much as by salt. Today barbecue cooks smoke meat mostly for flavour, but the smoke still works chemistry on the meat: it fights spoilage, paints a pink ring under the crust and, in its gentlest form, flavours food without ever cooking it.

On many American farms a century ago, a smokehouse stood out back, where hams and bacon hung for days over smouldering hardwood, and while the smoke gave the meat its deep flavour, its more valuable job was keeping the meat from spoiling, so a farm could store a year's worth of meat before refrigerators.

Among the hundreds of chemicals in smoke, a group called phenols collect on the meat's surface and fight spoilage twice over: as antimicrobials they slow bacteria and fungi, and as antioxidants they stop the fat from turning rancid.

Slice a smoked brisket and you often find a pink band about a quarter of an inch thick just below the dark crust. That smoke ring is not raw meat but a chemical mark: gases from the burning wood, mainly nitric oxide and carbon monoxide, soak into the surface and lock onto myoglobin, the meat's pigment, before the heat can brown it. Because the ring needs myoglobin, which is plentiful in red muscle, pale meat such as a chicken breast shows hardly any ring after smoking, while beef, wild game and heritage pork develop deep ones.

Smoked salmon and old-style bacon are cold-smoked, bathed in cool smoke that flavours them without cooking them, so they leave the smoker raw, and that is why they must be fully cured in salt before they ever meet the smoke. Hot-smoking, used for brisket and ribs, runs hot enough to cook the meat.

smoke-point-picking-the-right-fat-for-th.context_blurb:
Every cooking fat has a temperature at which it starts to smoke, and that number decides which fat belongs in which pan. A blazing sear needs a fat that can take the heat, while butter in that same pan quickly turns into a burnt mess, and even a costly olive oil can be ruined without a wisp of smoke.

As a pan of oil heats, it first shimmers; push the heat further and a thin, steady bluish haze rises, and the temperature where that begins is the smoke point, the sign that the fat is chemically breaking down and will start to taste burnt.

Butter is not pure fat: it also holds water and milk solids, the proteins whey and casein, and the brown, scorched specks in a hot butter pan are those milk proteins burning, which is why butter smokes at only about 150 to 190°C. For a deep fryer or a fierce sear, cooks reach for refined oils, because refining strips out the proteins, free fatty acids and flavour compounds that break down at low heat, and the champion among everyday oils is refined avocado oil, which holds out to about 271°C (520°F), far above butter.

Ghee in India and clarified butter in France are butter with the water and milk solids removed, so their smoke point leaps to about 250°C, high enough to sear without burning. To make it, the cook melts butter, skims off the whey proteins that rise and pours the clear golden fat away from the casein that sinks; ghee simmers longer so the solids turn nutty-brown first, and with no water left it also resists going rancid.

Extra-virgin olive oil smokes at about 190°C, but its prized flavour compounds and antioxidant polyphenols start breaking apart lower still, around 150 to 170°C, so even a gentle sauté with no smoke at all can destroy what you paid for. It is best drizzled raw or cooked over medium heat.

A smoke point is not fixed. Fryer oil used day after day cracks into more free fatty acids each session, so by the end of the week, dark as strong tea, it smokes at a lower heat than it did when fresh, which is why it is finally thrown out. Past the smoke point, the fat's glycerol turns into acrolein, a name built from acrid and the Latin for oil, the fume that stings your eyes over an over-hot pan.

solid-liquid-and-spoiling-saturated-mono.context_blurb:
Every cooking fat, from butter to olive oil, is built from long chains of carbon, and the shape of those chains explains nearly everything about it: whether it is solid or runny, whether it can stand a hot pan, how fast it spoils, and why one man-made fat was finally banned.

Butter stays solid on the counter while oil pours like water because butter is rich in saturated fat, whose chains are straight, so they stack together tightly and give it a high melting point; the chains of liquid oils are bent and cannot stack. Coconut oil is the extreme case: more than four-fifths of its fat is saturated, a bigger share than in butter or lard, so it stays solid or nearly so at room temperature and keeps a long time on the shelf.

That tight packing also makes saturated fats stable under heat and slow to spoil, which is why, before bottled vegetable oil took over, cooks deep-fried in lard and beef tallow, fats that could stand a blazing fryer without breaking down.

Polyunsaturated seed oils, such as unrefined sunflower and flaxseed, have chains with many double-bond kinks, and each kink is a weak spot where oxygen attacks when the oil is heated hard, so the oil turns rancid and harsh. Frying studies find that animal fats oxidise far less than polyunsaturated vegetable oils under repeated heating, which is why chefs sear in stable fats and save fragile oils for cold dressings; eaten unheated, those same oils lower LDL cholesterol in trials. Olive oil sits in the middle: it is monounsaturated, about three-quarters oleic acid, whose chain has just one kink, enough to keep it pourable but with far fewer weak spots than the seed oils, so it can handle a medium-hot pan.

In the early 1900s companies found a way to turn cheap, fast-spoiling liquid oil into a solid that kept for months: hydrogenation, forcing hydrogen gas into the oil to fill its double bonds and straighten its kinks. The German chemist Wilhelm Normann invented it in 1901 and patented it in 1902, and Crisco, launched in 1911, was the first shortening made entirely of hydrogenated vegetable oil.

To keep margarine spreadable, factories hydrogenated its oil only part of the way, which flipped many chains into a trans shape as a side effect. In a trans bond the two hydrogens sit on opposite sides of the double bond, which pulls the kink straight again, so the chains stack like a saturated fat and the spread stays solid and long-lasting. Partial hydrogenation turned about 40 percent of the fat into trans fat.

Butter's saturated fat raises LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, and its health effects are still argued over. Trans fat is plainly worse: it raises LDL too and also lowers HDL, the protective good cholesterol, a double harm to the heart. In 1993 Harvard's Nurses' Health Study linked the highest trans-fat intake to a 50 percent higher risk of heart disease, and from 2015 the FDA moved partially hydrogenated oils out of American food, with no new use after 2018.

sourdough-catching-wild-yeast-from-the-a.context_blurb:
A sourdough loaf needs no packet of yeast at all. Its baker keeps a starter, a living jar of flour and water full of wild yeast and bacteria, and feeds it for years, even generations, and one famous San Francisco starter has survived the Gold Rush, an earthquake and a city in flames.

When the Gold Rush brought fortune-seekers to San Francisco in 1849, the French baker Isidore Boudin opened a bakery near the waterfront. He raised his loaves with wild yeast and never a packet of the store-bought kind, and the bakery says the starter he began that year is still baked today. That wild yeast mostly rides in on the flour: in 2020 Aspen Reese and Robert Dunn found that the microbes of sourdough starters looked most like those living in the flour itself, with a share from the bakers' own hands. A starter, which bakers nickname the mother dough, is alive, and left alone for a few weeks its microbes starve and die, so it lives on steady meals of new flour and water; some famous starters have been fed on schedule for well over a century.

A starter is a partnership of two microbes: wild yeast makes the carbon-dioxide bubbles that raise the loaf, while lactic-acid bacteria make the sour tang. Packet yeast carries no acid-making bacteria, which is why its bread rises but never turns sour. The tang comes from two acids, mild lactic acid, the tang of yogurt, and sharp acetic acid, the bite of vinegar, and a starter kept cooler and drier builds up more acetic acid, so for the sharpest loaf the starter is kept cool and dry, and for a mild one, warm and wet.

When the earthquake of April 18, 1906, set San Francisco burning, Boudin family lore says Louise Boudin scooped the bakery's living mother dough into a wooden bucket and fled just before the fires destroyed the building, saving the starter begun in 1849. Boudin still adds a pinch of that dough to every loaf.

In 1971 a sourdough bacterium was even given San Francisco's name, and the city's bakers claimed their tang came from local air and water. But the Global Sourdough Project examined 500 starters gathered on four continents and found the same microbes turning up worldwide, with almost no link between where a baker lives and what lives in the starter, and the city-named bacterium thrives in traditional sourdoughs in France, Italy and China too.

soybeans-transformed-miso-soy-sauce-temp.context_blurb:
A plain soybean is small, hard and bland, yet whole cuisines across East and Southeast Asia are built on transformed soybeans. Miso, soy sauce, tofu, tempeh and natto all start as the same bean, worked on by a different microbe or technique, and the long ferments behind them unlock a savoury taste that a Japanese chemist named a little over a century ago.

Dark, salty miso paste, pale tofu as soft as custard and a firm slab of tempeh look and taste nothing alike, but all three are made from the soybean: miso is fermented soybean paste, tofu is curd pressed from soy milk, and tempeh is a cake of whole soybeans. Tempeh's chewy, meaty bite comes from keeping the cooked beans whole and intact, so that a mold can knit them into a firm cake in which you can still see each bean, while tofu's beans are ground up completely and their milk turned into soft curd.

Both miso and soy sauce sit fermenting in big vats for months or even years, guarded all that time by heavy salting: the salt pulls water out and makes the brine too harsh for spoilage microbes while the slow, flavour-building ferment carries on. Standard Japanese soy sauce is not made from soybeans alone, for roasted wheat makes up roughly half of the mix, whose starches ferment into sugars that balance the salty bean and add a toasty, faintly sweet aroma. Miso usually pairs its soybeans with a different grain.

Before any salt goes near them, miso and soy sauce makers deliberately grow a mold over the cooked beans and grain for a couple of days: koji, the fungus Aspergillus oryzae, the same mold that makes sake. Miso's colour tracks its age: pale white miso, fermented only briefly, stays sweet and mild, while dark red miso, aged a year or more, tastes much saltier and stronger, the choice for hearty winter stews.

Tempeh comes from a different country altogether: it was born on the island of Java, in Indonesia, where people have made it since around 1700, and it is bound by a different mold, Rhizopus, whose fine white threads knit the whole beans together.

The koji is there to work: as it spreads it releases enzymes, amylases that chop the beans' starch into simple sugars and proteases that chop their protein into amino acids, and those small pieces are what the long salty ferment develops into deep flavour. Natto, a sticky, strong-smelling breakfast food of Japan, is the odd one out, fermented not by a mold but by a bacterium, Bacillus subtilis, which turns boiled soybeans gluey and pungent and fills them with long, gooey strings that trail from the chopsticks.

The savoury punch of soy sauce, umami, is the taste of glutamate, and the ferment adds none of it. Soybeans are rich in protein, protein is built from amino acids including glutamate, and the enzymes cut the protein apart and set that glutamate free, so the savouriness was locked inside the soybean's protein all along. The same glutamate gives aged parmesan, ripe tomatoes and good broth their savoury depth.

The Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda traced the savoury taste of a plain broth simmered from dried kelp, kombu dashi, to glutamate, and in 1908 he named the taste umami, Japanese for pleasant savoury deliciousness. A year later he co-founded Ajinomoto and began selling purified glutamate as MSG.

spice-blends-the-merchants-secret-mixes.context_blurb:
Across Asia, the Middle East and Africa, cooks rarely reach for one spice at a time. They use blends, several spices ground together into a single seasoning, and many of the most famous, from Morocco's ras el hanout to Ethiopia's berbere, have no fixed recipe at all: each shop and family keeps its own, often never written down.

In the Levant, the Arabic word za'atar names two things at once: a wild aromatic herb, a cousin of oregano, thyme and marjoram, and the finished blend that cooks build around it and scatter over oiled flatbread. In Morocco's markets the great blend is ras el hanout, spooned into slow-cooked lamb tagines and over couscous, and its Arabic name means head of the shop: the top shelf, the very best spices the merchant has.

Classic za'atar is the dried herb, toasted sesame seeds and sumac, the dried, ground berries of a shrub, which give the blend its rust-red flecks and a sharp, lemony sourness that comes from malic acid, the acid that makes green apples tart. Sumac, by tradition, was the main souring spice of Middle Eastern and Roman cooks until lemons became common in the region and took over the job.

Every shop's ras el hanout tastes different, because there is no fixed recipe: each shop or family guards its own secret mix of a dozen or more spices, such as cardamom, cumin, clove, cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, coriander and turmeric, so one jar may smell of roses and another of warm pepper. Blend-makers toast whole seeds such as cumin and coriander in a dry, hot pan for about a minute before grinding, because the heat ruptures the seeds' cells and releases their aromatic oils, waking the flavour so that a toasted blend smells far stronger than one ground raw.

Some regional blends add rarer extras, such as dried rosebuds, grains of paradise and orris root.

Africa's two great blends of fire sit at opposite ends of the continent: Ethiopia's berbere, a dry, brick-red powder built on chili peppers and fenugreek with garlic, ginger and coriander, and Tunisia's harissa, a wet paste of roasted chili peppers, garlic, caraway, coriander and cumin loosened with olive oil. The burn in both comes from the one fiery ingredient they share, chili peppers. Both taste ancient, yet in their fiery modern form they are only about four centuries old, because chili peppers are native to the Americas and reached Africa only after Columbus's voyage of 1492.

spices-are-surprising-parts-of-a-plant.context_blurb:
Open a spice drawer and you see jars of look-alike powders and seeds, but every spice is one particular part of one particular plant, and the parts are wildly different: bark, berries, flower buds, threads from inside a flower, underground stems, pods and fruit. Working out which part is which turns the spice rack into a botany lesson.

Cinnamon is bark, the dried inner bark of the Cinnamomum tree: workers strip off the tough outer bark, pry the soft inner layer away in long strips, and as the strips dry they curl into the quills we call cinnamon sticks. A peppercorn is a berry, the fruit of the climbing vine Piper nigrum of India, a tiny stone fruit like a cherry that ripens red around one hard seed, and black peppercorns are those berries picked green and dried in the sun until their skins wrinkle black.

A clove is a flower bud: on the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, workers snip the small pink buds of the clove tree just before they open and dry them hard and brown. The dried bud, a long stem ending in a little ball, looks so like a nail that its name comes from the Latin clavus, nail. The clove tree once grew wild only on that cluster of volcanic islands, which together with nutmeg made them the world's only source of both spices, so Europeans called them the Spice Islands, and Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and English fleets fought over them for centuries.

White pepper comes from the same vine as black: the berry is left to ripen, then its dark outer skin is soaked and rubbed off, leaving the pale seed inside, while green pepper is the unripe berry kept green in brine or by freeze-drying. A caper is a flower bud too, picked from a spiny Mediterranean bush that grows on cliffs and old walls; workers pinch off the tightest green buds before dawn, before they open, and the smaller the bud, the pricier the caper, while a bud left to bloom and set fruit becomes a larger caperberry.

Saffron, the costliest spice of all, is three slender red threads, the stigmas, plucked by hand from the centre of each crocus flower; some 150,000 flowers go into one kilogram, which often sells for more than $5,000. Ginger is not a root at all but a stem: a rhizome, which creeps sideways below the surface, sending leafy shoots up and thin roots down, something a true root cannot do, and its golden cousin turmeric, coloured by curcumin, grows the same way.

Most supermarket cinnamon, the hard, dark, tightly curled kind, is really cassia, a cheaper cousin with thick bark, while true Ceylon cinnamon is pale and made of thin, papery layers that crumble in the hand; cassia also carries far more coumarin, which can strain the liver in large daily amounts.

Vanilla, the second-priciest spice, is the cured pod of a climbing orchid native to Mexico, and grown elsewhere it has no natural pollinator, so workers fertilise each one-day flower by hand within about twelve hours of its opening. Cardamom, third in price after saffron and vanilla, comes in small, three-sided green pods, but the pod is mostly a wrapper: the spice is the cluster of tiny black-brown seeds inside, freed by splitting the pod open.

Sweet paprika, chili powder and fiery cayenne are all the dried, ground fruit of Capsicum plants, which botanists count as berries, grown in varieties bred for different heat; on the Scoville scale a bell pepper rates zero and a jalapeño about 4,000 to 8,000. Most cooks believe a chili's fire lives in its seeds, but food scientists say the capsaicin is packed into the white pith, the inner membrane that holds the seeds in place. Birds feel no burn from capsaicin while mammals do, so birds eat the fruit and scatter the seeds whole, while mammals, which would grind the seeds up, leave the fruit alone.

squid-and-octopus-rubbery-or-tender-neve.context_blurb:
Squid and octopus, the soft-bodied cousins of the sea, are tender and mild when raw yet turn to rubber bands after a moment of careless cooking. They follow a strange rule shared by few other foods: cook them for seconds or for hours, because almost nothing in between works.

Calamari is simply Italian for squid: the crispy fried rings are slices cut across the squid's tube-shaped body, the mantle, and the little curly pieces in the basket are its arms.

Both animals stay tender only when cooked very fast or very slow, either a quick flash over high heat lasting no more than about two minutes or a long, slow braise of at least half an hour, while anything in the middle turns them to rubber.

Fishermen in Greece and Italy have long used a hands-on shortcut, told as tradition. As soon as the boat reaches the harbour, the fisherman grabs a fresh octopus and slams it again and again against the rocks of the pier, about forty times and up to a hundred for some, smashing the tough muscle fibres and driving out water. That beating does by hand what a slow braise later does with heat, and Japanese cooks use the same trick.

The rubber comes from muscle: squid muscle contracts fast when heated, so rings that leave a very hot pan within a minute or two are pulled off before their proteins tighten, but linger a minute longer and the muscle fibres clench and wring out the water, leaving the rings dry and springy.

The slow route works differently: like a cheap, hard-working cut of beef such as shank, octopus is full of tough connective tissue, collagen, and only long, low, moist heat, about an hour of gentle simmering, melts that collagen into soft, silky gelatin. A quick sear never gets there.

stalks-and-shoots-the-stems-and-leaf-sta.context_blurb:
Some favourite vegetables are neither roots nor leaves but the parts in between: stems, and the stalks that hold leaves up to the sun. Asparagus, celery, rhubarb and kohlrabi are each cut for one particular part at one particular stage, which explains how they look, why some are white instead of green, and why some of their leaves go in the bin.

An asparagus spear is a young, fast-growing stem, snapped off in spring while it is short and tender; left uncut, it shoots upward and ferns out into a tall, feathery plant about three to five feet high, which is why growers cut spears before they turn woody. The tight, scaly tip that chefs prize as the tenderest part of a spear is the plant's folded-up baby foliage, tiny scale leaves that would open into needle-like green shoots as the spear ferns out, so spears must be picked before the tip starts to open.

White asparagus, sold in German and French spring markets at twice the price of green, comes from the very same plant: growers heap soil over the shoots so no sunlight reaches them, and with no light the spears make no green chlorophyll and stay pale.

Celery is not a stem at all but a leaf-stalk, which botanists call a petiole, the part whose job is to hold a leaf out to catch the sun; the tough strings you peel are bundles of cells running along its water tubes, which carry water up the stalk and stiffen it. Rhubarb is a leaf-stalk too, so tart that cooks stew it with sugar like a fruit. Its big leaves, however, are always cut off and thrown away because they are toxic, packed with oxalic acid, a poison that damages the kidneys, though a person would have to eat a lot of leaf to be badly harmed.

Kohlrabi, a fist-sized pale bulb sprouting leafy stalks, is a stem that grows swollen and round above the soil, proof that a vegetable sold among the roots can be a stem. Its German name means cabbage-turnip, and it belongs to the same species as cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale and Brussels sprouts, wild cabbage that people bred into many different shapes.

stir-fry-logic-and-velveting.context_blurb:
A Chinese stir-fry is cooked fast, hard and hot: food sliced thin, a wok heated until it smokes, and nothing left in the pan for long. Its rules all follow from that fierce heat, and Chinese cooks add a trick called velveting that gives restaurant meat a silkiness home cooks struggle to match.

A stir-fry cooks in only two or three minutes over ferocious heat, so there is no time to chop or measure once the wok is hot, and cooks have every vegetable cut, the meat marinated and the sauce waiting in bowls before they begin. Ingredients then go in by a strict order: garlic and ginger first, to flavour the oil, then the meat, then the sturdier vegetables, and the sauce last of all, so every piece finishes cooked but still crisp.

The prize of a great stir-fry is wok hei, a Cantonese name meaning breath of the wok: the smoky, scorched fragrance that appears only when food hits metal at blazing heat, which Cantonese chefs treat as the soul of the dish and a weak home stove struggles to make.

Overcrowding ruins all of it: overload the wok with chilly, damp ingredients and the temperature plunges, so the heat's energy goes into boiling off surface water and the food steams to a soft, grey heap rather than browning. Cooks fill no more than about a third of the wok, let it reheat for 30 to 45 seconds between batches and pat vegetables dry.

Velveting coats raw slices of meat in cornstarch, often with a little egg white and oil, forming a slick shell that seals in the juices and shields the meat from the fierce heat. The coated meat is briefly pre-cooked in hot water or warm oil, so the final toss in the wok only has to finish it.

Restaurant cooks go one step further with a little baking soda. Beef starts out slightly acidic, and in the more alkaline setting the soda creates, its proteins cannot bond and clench as tightly when heated, so the fibres stay relaxed instead of wringing out their juice, and even cheap, tough chuck stays tender in a two-minute stir-fry. Too much leaves the meat soapy and bitter, so cooks use only a sprinkle and rinse it well.

stock-fond-and-mirepoix.context_blurb:
Behind every classical French soup and sauce stands a pot of bones, vegetables and water left to simmer gently for hours on a quiet corner of the stove. French cooks treat that humble pot as the base of everything they make, and the chopped vegetables that start it carry the name of an eighteenth-century nobleman.

In English this long-simmered liquid is called stock: bones and vegetables covered with water and cooked low and slow for hours until their flavour and body pass into the liquid, which becomes the base for countless soups and sauces. French cooks call it fond, short for fonds de cuisine, which means the foundation of the kitchen, its working capital, the base under everything else a chef builds.

Most French stocks, soups and braises start with a mirepoix: diced onion, carrot and celery, classically twice as much onion as either of the others, softened gently in fat so they turn sweet rather than brown.

A good meat stock chilled overnight sets into a wobbly jelly, because hours of gentle simmering turn the collagen in bones and connective tissue into gelatin, which dissolves into the liquid and gives stock its lip-coating body. The same bones make two different stocks: a pale, clean-tasting white stock, fond blanc, starts from raw bones, while a dark amber brown stock, fond brun, is made by roasting the bones and mirepoix in a hot oven first, often with a coat of tomato paste, before any water goes in.

Keep the pot at a bare simmer, never a rolling boil: violent bubbles act like a blender, whipping the melted fat and the floating protein scum back into the liquid so the stock turns cloudy and greasy, while a gentle simmer lets them float up where the cook can skim them off.

The richest use of brown stock is demi-glace, "half glaze": classically equal parts brown stock and espagnole sauce reduced by half into a dark, shiny syrup that coats a spoon. Auguste Escoffier set it down in Le Guide Culinaire, which appeared in English in 1907 as A Guide to Modern Cookery.

One last story belongs to the mirepoix. It takes its name from the duc de Lévis-Mirepoix, an 18th-century French field marshal, but the writer Pierre Larousse scorned the duke as incompetent and mediocre, a man whose one claim to fame was lending his name to a sauce, and the story goes that his cook, not the duke, actually created it.

subtleties-and-sugar-at-the-table.context_blurb:
At the great feasts of medieval and Renaissance Europe, the most spectacular dish might be a castle, a ship or a swan made of sugar and almond paste. Sugar was rare and costly then, so these edible sculptures, called subtleties, let a rich host show off his fortune, and their story ends when sugar became cheap.

Subtleties, also spelled sotelties, were paraded between courses as pure spectacle, a castle with tiny towers and soldiers, a ship or a beast, and since they were sculpted from food, the guests ate them once they had finished marvelling. Confectioners built the castles from marzipan, which old English cookbooks spelled marchpane: ground almonds worked with sugar into a stiff paste, a sweet clay that could be molded into fruit, animals, coins or towers.

Not every subtlety was sugar. Renaissance cooks baked pies holding live birds that flew out when the crust was cut, and tradition ties the trick to the nursery rhyme Sing a Song of Sixpence, whose blackbirds, four and twenty of them, begin to sing when the pie is opened.

Sugar reached medieval Europe as a medicine and a spice, in small, precious lumps from Arab lands, dearer by weight than many spices, and anyone in a medieval city who wanted a spoonful had to buy it from the apothecary, the medieval druggist, since physicians prized it as hot and moist, almost a miracle food.

Great Tudor houses even built a separate little room for the sweets, the banqueting house, where the host led only his favoured guests; some were tiny, one at Lacock Abbey seating only six, and many stood up on the rooftop, as at Longleat, which carried seven on its roofs. In Tudor England the word banquet itself meant something small: not a whole feast but the sweet finale at the end of the meal, sugared fruits, comfits and spiced wine served after everything else was cleared, and only later did the word swell to mean the entire grand dinner.

Subtleties could also carry a message. When the boy king Henry VI was crowned in 1429, every course of the feast in Westminster Hall brought a sugar statue pressing his royal claims. One showed Henry between Saint Edward, England's royal saint, and Saint Louis of France, claiming the crown of France as well as England's, with verses by the monk-poet John Lydgate.

The showpiece's power rested on scarcity. Once Brazilian and Caribbean plantations sent sugar to Europe in such quantities in the 1600s and 1700s that ordinary families could afford it, a sugar castle no longer proved a host was rich, so the subtlety could no longer impress anyone and quietly faded from the table.

sugar-cane-beet-and-what-refining-does.context_blurb:
White sugar can come from two completely different plants grown in opposite climates, a giant tropical grass and a pale northern root, yet both end up as the same crystal in the bowl. How each is turned into sugar, and how much of its dark syrup is left behind, explains every sugar on the baking shelf.

Sugarcane is a grass, a giant perennial one that grows on stout, jointed stalks six metres or more tall in fields from Brazil to India, and chewing a piece of raw cane squeezes its sweet juice out between your teeth. The other source, the sugar beet, thrives where winters are cold, and unlike the red beets people roast, its root is pale white inside.

Brown sugar begins as ordinary refined white sugar with a little molasses, the dark, sticky syrup, stirred back in; dark brown sugar simply gets more molasses than light brown.

The two plants are processed differently: a cane mill crushes the stalks to squeeze out the juice, but a beet factory cuts the hard roots into thin strips, known as cossettes, and soaks them in hot water, about 70 to 75°C, so the sugar dissolves out into the water.

Sugar is not a European invention. Papuan farmers on New Guinea first tamed sugarcane about 6,000 years ago, breeding it from a wild grass, and only much later did it travel west to India. In India, around 350 AD, people first learned to boil cane juice down and crystallise it into storable grains, and the English word sugar descends from their Sanskrit word sharkara, which first meant grit or gravel, after the look of the little crystals.

Refined, cane and beet give the identical molecule, sucrose, so the body cannot tell the two apart and only a lab test of carbon isotopes can; each sucrose molecule is a pair of simpler sugars linked as one, a glucose and a fructose.

The specialty brown sugars differ in how much molasses stays on the crystals: turbinado, from the first pressing, keeps only a little, while muscovado, prized in British desserts, is the darkest and moistest, with the most molasses and the strongest flavour.

sugar-the-sweet-that-crossed-the-ocean.context_blurb:
Sugar began as a sweet grass chewed on a tropical island, became a medicine sold by the pinch in medieval Europe, and then crossed the Atlantic, where planters built an industry on the forced labour of enslaved Africans. Cheap sugar changed how the whole world eats, and its story runs from New Guinea to the plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean.

Sugarcane's original home is New Guinea, where people first chewed the wild stalks and then domesticated the plant around 4000 BC; it spread slowly west through Asia to India, where people first learned to boil the juice down into solid sugar.

In medieval Europe the only common sweetener was honey, made by bees, while sugar was a rare, costly import treated more like an exotic spice than a pantry staple. Europeans bought it by the pinch at the apothecary, and only monarchs and the very rich could afford it.

Christopher Columbus brought sugarcane to the Americas on his second voyage in 1493, carrying cuttings from the Canary Islands to Hispaniola, a crop moving the opposite way from the potatoes, tomatoes, corn and cocoa that sailed from the Americas to Europe.

In the 1500s Portuguese settlers made Brazil the first sugar giant of the Americas: it had about 60 mills by 1570 and some 120 by the mid-1580s, most in Pernambuco and Bahia, worked by enslaved Africans whom the planters forced into the fields. Shiploads of Brazilian sugar went to Europe, where they sweetened the bitter new drinks of tea, coffee and hot chocolate.

The mills and boiling houses ran day and night, six days a week, because cane must be crushed and its juice boiled within about a day of cutting, or the stalks spoil and the juice will no longer set into crystals. Planters forced that relentless, dangerous work on enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic to the plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean.

sugar-vs-fat-who-was-the-real-villain.context_blurb:
In the mid-1900s, as heart attacks climbed, scientists fought over the culprit. The American Ancel Keys blamed saturated fat; the Briton John Yudkin blamed sugar. Keys won the public argument for decades, but a hidden-funding scandal, a viral lecture and a fresh look at the old data have since reopened the case, and both questions are still argued today.

Ancel Keys persuaded Americans, and in time their government too, that saturated fat, above all the animal fat in butter, red meat and eggs, lay behind most heart attacks, and for decades reduced-fat and lite foods filled the shelves while sugar got a pass. John Yudkin broke ranks, arguing that sugar drove heart disease, diabetes and tooth decay, and in 1972 he set out his argument in a book titled Pure, White and Deadly, published in America as Sweet and Dangerous; at the time almost no one believed him.

The low-fat craze of the 1980s and 1990s backfired: fat carries flavour and richness, so fat-free cookies, yogurts and dressings tasted dull, and manufacturers pumped in sugar and starch to rescue them, which meant low-fat rarely meant low-calorie. The face of the craze was SnackWell's, Nabisco's fat-free cookies in a green box, and because fat-free felt like permission, people ate the whole box and swallowed just as many calories as ordinary cookies held, a trap nicknamed the SnackWell's effect. By 2022 most SnackWell's products had been discontinued.

In 2016 researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, Cristin Kearns, Laura Schmidt and Stanton Glantz, published documents showing why the science had tilted: in the 1960s the sugar industry's Sugar Research Foundation had secretly paid three Harvard scientists about $6,500, nearly $49,000 in 2016 dollars, to publish a review blaming fat and playing down sugar. After reading the draft, the foundation's vice-president, John Hickson, wrote to assure the scientists that this was quite what the industry had in mind, and the review ran in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1967 with no word about who had paid for it.

By the early 2000s the low-fat era was collapsing, and a rival fad swept America: the Atkins diet of the New York cardiologist Robert Atkins, high in fat and low in carbohydrates, with bacon, butter, cheese and steak in and bread, pasta and sweets out. Yudkin was nearly forgotten when he died in 1995, but in 2009 Robert Lustig, a doctor in California, delivered a lecture called Sugar: The Bitter Truth that reached tens of millions of viewers online and revived Yudkin's warning. When Yudkin's book was reissued in 2012, Lustig wrote the foreword and called himself a proud Yudkin disciple.

Today sugar is widely seen as one cause of weight gain, diabetes and heart trouble, which partly vindicates Yudkin, and the evidence is strongest against sugary sodas and drinks, since liquid sugar is so easy to overdo.

Yet the case has no single villain. A chart in that same 1967 review, which the food-policy scientist Marion Nestle reprinted in 2016, showed sugar and saturated fat across 14 countries tangled together, impossible to separate, both rising with the deaths from heart disease. Fat was over-blamed and sugar got an undeserved pass, but both questions stay open: mainstream bodies still count saturated fat as a heart risk, meta-analyses in 2010 and 2014 failed to confirm that link, and scientists still debate how much sugar itself, as against plain overeating, drives disease.

sugars-hidden-jobs-beyond-sweetness.context_blurb:
A baker who cuts the sugar out of a cake finds it is not just less sweet but tougher, drier, paler and quicker to go stale. Sugar does a string of hidden jobs in food that have nothing to do with taste: it holds water, softens crumbs, feeds yeast, browns crusts, smells of butter and keeps ice cream scoopable.

Sugar is hygroscopic: it grabs water molecules and clings to them, so the water cannot evaporate away, which is why a sugary pound cake stays soft for days while a lean baguette goes hard by the next morning. Sugar also competes with flour for water, so the flour's proteins cannot link up into as much gluten, the stretchy, chewy network, while the dough is mixed, and a sugary shortbread bakes meltingly tender while a low-sugar one turns tough.

In bread dough a spoonful of sugar is the yeast's fast first food: the yeast digests it before the flour's starch and gives off carbon dioxide, whose bubbles puff up the dough, along with a little alcohol, so the dough starts rising sooner.

There are two routes by which sugar browns a bake: caramelising, sugar alone darkening in the heat, and the Maillard reaction, in which sugar reacts with protein from the eggs, milk and flour to build a deep golden crust, so cutting the sugar leaves cookies and cake tops pale.

Too much sugar slows yeast down: in a very sweet brioche dough the sugar draws water out of the yeast cells by osmosis until they shrivel, just as heavy salt does, so a little sugar, under about 3 percent of the flour, speeds the yeast while more than about 5 percent holds it back. Bakers use special osmotolerant yeast for brioche, panettone and doughnuts. Melt plain white sugar into caramel and it smells of butter, because as it darkens it forms diacetyl, the very molecule that gives real butter its buttery flavour.

Sugar also lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so at freezer temperature much of the water in ice cream never turns solid but stays a concentrated syrup, which keeps it scoopable while an ice cube sets rock-hard. More sugar means a softer freeze, and sorbet works the same way.

supertasters-and-the-bitter-gene.context_blurb:
Roughly one person in four is a supertaster, someone whose tongue feels bitterness far more sharply than average. Supertasters often turn down dark chocolate, strong coffee and greens such as broccoli and kale, and the trait is inherited through a bitter-taste gene whose receptor turns out to work far beyond the tongue.

The story often told is that in 1931 the chemist Arthur Fox let a bitter powder, PTC, escape into his laboratory's air: a colleague complained of the awful bitter taste, while Fox, standing right beside it, tasted nothing at all. The accident revealed that people split into tasters and nontasters, and paper strips soaked in PTC or its milder cousin PROP still identify supertasters today.

The same bitter compounds found in broccoli, kale and Brussels sprouts turn up in grapefruit, so the sensitive receptor that supertasters carry makes grapefruit taste especially sharp to them.

Children feel bitterness even more keenly than adults who carry the same gene, and the sharpness does not settle to adult levels until the middle or late teenage years; scientists think it evolved so that toddlers would spit out a poisonous plant, at an age when a wandering child might grab and swallow one.

The bitter receptor behind it, TAS2R38, also lines the nose, airways and sinuses, and when it senses the bitter chemicals that invading bacteria release, it fires off a burst of nitric oxide, a germ-killing gas, so a taste receptor doubles as part of the body's defences.

surstromming-the-can-that-bulges.context_blurb:
Surströmming is Sweden's famously pungent sour herring, sold in tins that bulge outward as if about to burst. In any other canned food that swelling would warn of danger, but here it marks a good tin, and the reason lies in a ferment that never stops.

The lightly salted herring ferments for months in barrels and then keeps fermenting inside the sealed can, where live bacteria go on making carbon dioxide and other gases that have nowhere to escape, so the metal swells outward.

Because that gas puts the tin under real pressure, Swedes open it outdoors, traditionally puncturing it while it is held underwater in a bucket so the water catches the spray of foul brine. In 2006 several big airlines, among them Air France and British Airways, banned the tins from flights as possibly explosive.

Its makers insist it is not rotten fish but a controlled ferment. The control is the salt: a weak brine strong enough to block the dangerous spoilage bacteria but mild enough to let the fermenting microbes keep working, since more salt would stop the ferment and less would let the fish truly rot. Unlike Iceland's fermented shark, hákarl, which is fermented to drive off a poison, Baltic herring is not poisonous, so its souring is purely for flavour.

sushi-from-preservation-to-nigiri.context_blurb:
Sushi today means fresh raw fish on little mounds of seasoned rice, but for most of its long history it was something else entirely: a way of keeping fish by packing it in rice and leaving it to sour for months. The modern hand-pressed form is a much later Japanese shortcut, and the old style still survives.

Sushi is named for its rice, not its fish: the seasoned rice base is what makes a dish sushi, plenty of sushi contains no fish at all, and the word itself traces back to an old term meaning sour. The most familiar form is nigiri, from a word meaning to grip or press: the chef presses a pinch of vinegared rice into a small oval in his palm and lays a single slice of fish, the neta, over the top.

The first sushi, more than a thousand years ago, was not a treat but a way of keeping fish from spoiling: souring fish in salt and rice kept a catch edible for months, long before refrigerators.

The old method layered salted fish with cooked rice in a stone-weighted barrel for months, and when it was opened the soured rice went in the bin; only the fish was eaten, and eating the rice came centuries later. In the Edo period, impatient cooks found a shortcut, haya-zushi or fast sushi: they mixed rice vinegar into the rice to give the same sour tang with no waiting, so the fish could be eaten the same day, which is why sushi rice is still vinegared.

The throw-away-the-rice style survives as funazushi, made around Lake Biwa: crucian carp salted and packed in rice to ferment for months, sometimes up to three years. Japan's oldest surviving kind of sushi, it has a pungent smell like strong cheese.

The dab of wasabi between rice and fish does more than add heat: it contains allyl isothiocyanate, a compound that kills spoilage-causing microbes, a natural safety match for raw fish before refrigeration. The pickled ginger, gari, beside the sushi was used the same way.

tadka-tempering-blooming-spices-in-fat.context_blurb:
Many Indian curries and dals start, or finish, with a small ritual at the stove: a spoonful of ghee or oil heated in a little pan, whole spices dropped in to sizzle and pop, and the fragrant fat poured into the dish. The step has a name, and the chemistry behind it explains why it matters so much.

The technique is tadka, also called tarka, chaunk, baghaar or vaghar in different parts of India: whole spices such as black mustard seeds, cumin, dried red chilies and curry leaves bloomed in hot fat, either at the start of cooking or spooned over a finished dal as a crowning flourish. Cooks never skip it, and a Hindi saying explains why: without tadka, everything is pheeka, tasteless or bland.

Fat works better than water because a spice's flavour sits in essential oils, compounds such as cuminaldehyde and eugenol, which dissolve readily in fat but hardly in water, and the flavoured fat then carries that taste through every lentil and grain of rice it coats. South Indian cooks often finish a tadka with fresh curry leaves from the curry tree, which crackle and crisp in about fifteen seconds and release an aroma bright like citrus, a surprise from a dark-green leaf.

Whole spices smell faint because their fragrant oils are sealed within the tough walls of the seed's cells: grinding cracks those walls open, and so does the heat of the tadka, which frees the oils at about 180 to 200°C, with only ten to twenty seconds between blooming and burning.

Bengal's tempering blend, panch phoron, five spices of fennel, cumin, black mustard, fenugreek and nigella, is unusual among Indian mixes because it is always used whole, never ground, popped in hot fat until the seeds crackle. Each region blooms its tadka in its own local fat, tied to the oil crops that grow nearby, and in Kerala, in the far south-west, that fat is coconut oil.

Timing depends on form: hard whole seeds such as mustard and cumin go in early and bloom for a minute or more, while a fine powder such as garam masala waits until the last moment, because in plain hot oil a fine powder burns bitter in a matter of seconds and loses its aroma. Black mustard seeds must actually pop to work: the moisture inside each seed flashes into steam, which bursts the seed and sprays its oils into the fat, and the popping tells the cook the oil is hot enough for the other spices.

Raw asafoetida, the dried resin called hing, smells harshly of sulphur and medicine, but bloomed in hot fat for under about fifteen seconds, before any liquid goes in, its harsh compounds turn into a savoury, almost meaty umami, like slow-cooked onions and garlic. Leave cumin in the hot ghee until it darkens and the Maillard reaction, the same browning that gives a seared steak its crust, invents new flavours the raw seed never had: roasty pyrazines, caramel-like furans and a nutty note like toasted almond skin. Flavour is created, not merely drawn out.

Tadka even helps the body. Turmeric's yellow pigment, curcumin, dissolves in fat too, so turmeric cooked in hot ghee is easier for the body to absorb, and a pinch of black pepper boosts absorption further still. In one human study, curcumin taken with piperine, the active compound in black pepper, was absorbed about 2,000 percent better, because piperine blocks the liver enzymes that would otherwise clear curcumin out before the body can use it.

taming-the-first-food-animals.context_blurb:
Some ten millennia back, across the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East, people began keeping animals instead of only hunting them. Goats, sheep, cattle and pigs came first, each tamed from a wild ancestor, and the changes herders made to their animals still shape what is on our plates.

The very first livestock were goats and sheep, small herd animals that live on rough plants people cannot digest, kept in pens some 10,500 years ago; cattle and pigs followed soon after in the same region. Every cow alive descends from the aurochs, a separate, now-extinct species of huge wild ox with a black coat and long horns, hunted since the Stone Age and painted on the cave walls of Lascaux, and the last one died in a Polish forest in 1627.

Sheep descend from a wild animal that still lives: the mouflon, a mountain sheep with curling horns, domesticated in Mesopotamia between roughly 11,000 and 9000 BC.

A bull aurochs weighed about 700 kilograms and carried horns up to 80 centimetres long that swept forward, curving inward toward each other like the arms of a lyre, a small harp. Julius Caesar, who met aurochs in the Hercynian forest, wrote that they spared neither man nor beast they spotted, though he wildly exaggerated their size.

Wild boar became the farm pig twice over, quite independently: first by Near Eastern farmers some ten millennia back, and then by Chinese farmers roughly two thousand years later, who had no contact with the first herders, started from their own wild boar and did the whole job a second time.

The first domestic sheep had no fleece at all: they were hairy, kept for meat, milk and skins, and herders bred wool into their flocks over thousands of years, selecting woolly animals perhaps from around 6000 BC until the first woven wool clothes appeared around 4000 BC.

Most animals could never be tamed: of the world's 148 large wild plant-eating land mammals, only 14 became livestock. The zebra is the famous failure in Jared Diamond's account, for besides biting and refusing a human as herd leader, it suffers a panic so violent, bred into it by heavy lion predation, that a captured zebra can panic itself to death in a pen.

Herding shows up in people's choices before it shows in the animals' bodies. At the Zagros site of Ganj Dareh, goat bones about ten thousand years old still look wild, but Melinda Zeder and Brian Hesse read the kill pattern: young males taken for meat and females kept alive into old age, the mark of herders protecting the breeding stock that makes next year's herd.

taste-modifiers-molecules-that-hijack-yo.context_blurb:
A few plant molecules can rewire how the tongue reports taste. A West African berry makes sour foods taste sweet for an hour, an Indian leaf makes sugar taste of nothing, and a chemical in ordinary toothpaste ruins orange juice every morning. Each works by tampering with the tongue's sweet sensors.

The miracle fruit, also called the miracle berry, is a small red West African berry about two centimetres long; chew one and for an hour or two every sour food tastes sweet, so a raw lemon becomes lemonade and vinegar tastes like apple juice.

The berry adds no sugar to the food. It briefly retunes the tongue's sweet sensors so that the very same lemon now reads as sweet, and the effect wears off on its own; in the early 1970s the American Robert Harvey's company, Miralin, even tried to sell miracle-fruit tablets as a sweetener with no calories.

India has the mirror image, a climbing vine called Gymnema sylvestre whose leaf is nicknamed gurmar, sugar-destroyer: its gymnemic acids block the sweet sensors, so a spoonful of sugar tastes like flavourless grit, like a mouthful of sand, until the block wears off after 15 to 50 minutes.

Orange juice after brushing your teeth tastes bitter and sour because of the toothpaste's foaming agent, the detergent sodium lauryl sulfate that makes it lather: it mutes the sweet sensors and also breaks up fatty molecules on the tongue that normally hold bitterness down, an effect that fades within a few minutes.

temperature-and-fizz-change-the-taste.context_blurb:
The same food can taste very different depending on how cold or fizzy it is. Melted ice cream tastes sickly, iced tea seems barely sweet, and soda can go dead in the mouth, and scientists have traced each effect to what happens on the tongue and along the nerves to the brain.

Ice cream makers pack in extra sugar on purpose so a frozen scoop does not taste bland, and that extra sugar only shows up once the dessert warms, which is why a melted bowl tastes like syrup; warm, flat cola tastes cloying for the same reason.

Cold does not switch the sweet sensors off but muffles their message: biologists studying fruit flies, whose taste wiring resembles our own, found that cool temperatures rouse other taste neurons, which send a signal that hushes the sweet neurons before their report reaches the brain. Warmth does the opposite, since the sweet-signal channel TRPM5 grows far more active as the tongue warms from about 15 to 35°C.

Fizz is tasted, not merely felt. Climbers taking the altitude pill acetazolamide complain of the champagne blues, bubbly drinks gone dead, and Charles Zuker's team traced it to an enzyme the pill blocks, carbonic anhydrase 4, which sits on the sour taste cells and turns a drink's dissolved carbon dioxide into acid so the sour cells taste the fizz.

tempura-the-portuguese-gift-to-japan.context_blurb:
Tempura, Japan's featherlight battered shrimp and vegetables, feels as Japanese as sushi, yet it arrived from Europe. Catholic missionaries brought the batter-and-fry technique, and probably the name, in the 1500s, and Japanese cooks then perfected a batter so delicate it fries into lace.

Portuguese missionaries, Jesuits who landed at Nagasaki in the 16th century through the trade the Japanese called Nanban, brought the technique of dipping food in batter and deep-frying it, so a dish that tastes thoroughly Japanese is a roughly 400-year-old European import.

The leading theory traces the name to the Latin tempora, times, meaning the fasting days of the Catholic calendar, the Ember Days and Lent, when meat was forbidden and the missionaries ate battered, fried fish and vegetables instead; some scholars trace it instead to the Portuguese tempero, a seasoning.

A tempura master makes the batter with ice-cold water and barely stirs it, a few flicks of chopsticks that leave it lumpy, because stirring flour and water builds gluten, the stretchy wheat protein that makes a coating chewy. With little gluten, the batter fries into crisp, airy lace instead of a thick, doughy jacket.

thai-curry-pastes-why-green-out-burns-re.context_blurb:
Thai curries are named by colour, red, green and yellow, plus the brown Massaman, and every one starts with a paste pounded by hand from fresh herbs and chilies. The colours hide two surprises: the gentle-looking green is usually the hottest, and the mildest of all came from far across the sea.

A Thai cook pounds galangal, lemongrass and chilies in a heavy stone mortar, and the pounding bruises the plants and bursts their cells, squeezing out fragrant essential oils that a jar of dry powder can never give. The colour comes from the chilies the cook pounds in, with no dye at all: green curry from fresh green chilies, red curry from dried red ones.

Green paste uses fresh green chilies straight off the plant, along with fresh coriander, makrut lime and Thai basil, but the big red chilies for red paste come only dried, so the cook first soaks them in warm water until they turn soft and pliable.

Diners expect the crimson red curry to burn hardest, but green curry usually bites harder, because fresh green chilies hit hard and fast while dried red chilies mellow and sweeten as they soak. That holds for traditional pastes; jarred supermarket brands vary.

Massaman is the odd one out, mild, sweet and slow, and packed with warm dried spices such as cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, cumin and nutmeg that are foreign to most Thai cooking and belong to Indian and Middle Eastern kitchens. Its name tells its story: massaman is a Thai reshaping of the Persian mosalman, meaning Muslim, once written Mussulman in English, and Persian and Muslim traders brought the dish and its spices to Ayutthaya's royal court during the 1600s.

The last secret is to sizzle the paste in hot fat from the coconut before any liquid goes in, just as an Indian cook blooms spices in a tadka: the heat dissolves the spices' oil-based aromas and spreads them through the dish, while paste stirred cold into liquid stays harsh. Cooks get that fat by cracking the coconut cream, simmering thick cream until its water boils away and the oil splits out.

thai-flavor-balance-four-tastes-in-one-b.context_blurb:
Thai cooks do not let one flavour lead. They balance several tastes on the tongue at once, adjusting bite by bite, and that balance runs from the sauces in the pan to the dishes on the table and even to the little pots beside a bowl of noodles.

Where Western cooks count sweet, sour, salty and bitter as the basic four, Thai cooking swaps bitter for chili heat, prizing sweet, sour, salty and spicy, and the goal is balance, with no single taste allowed to bully the others. Some Thai cooks keep bitter as a fifth.

For salt, a Thai cook reaches not for the shaker but for fish sauce, nam pla, which carries a deep, savoury umami from natural glutamate along with its saltiness. It is made from tiny ocean fish, often anchovies, packed with plenty of salt and fermented for six to twelve months in the tropical heat, and the brown liquid that seeps out is the sauce.

For sweetness the cook uses palm sugar, the boiled-down sap of coconut and sugar palms, a soft, sticky tan paste with a faint caramel taste that softens the heat and sour edge of a dish as well as sweetening it.

A full Thai meal is not one plate but four or more dishes served together, often a curry, a salad, a soup and something fried, so that the balance of sweet, sour, salty and hot runs across the whole table, not just one bite.

Even a finished bowl of noodle soup comes with the kruang prung, a caddy of four small pots, one for each taste: fish sauce with chilies for salty, sugar for sweet, dried-chili flakes for heat and chilies in vinegar for sour. Spooning from them, the diner finishes the flavour balance the cook began.

Tom yum soup adds a fifth layer on top of the four tastes: stalks of lemongrass, coins of galangal, a sharp, piney cousin of ginger, and torn makrut lime leaves, which diners push aside rather than eat, because their only job is to fill the broth with scent.

the-56-disguises-of-sugar.context_blurb:
Food labels do not always say sugar. Companies can list it under dozens of other names, and a careful shopper learns to spot them, along with a few rules for reading the label and an honest picture of what scientists agree on and what they still argue about.

Sugar in whole fruit is not the same as sugar in soda: two apples hold about as much as a can, but the apple's sugar comes wrapped in fibre and water, which slow its absorption and soften the spike, while soda is sugar-water that rushes into the blood within minutes. That is why nutrition guidelines target added sugar, not the sugar built into whole fruit.

The World Health Organization groups the sugars worth cutting back as free sugars: those that factories add, plus honey, syrups and fruit juice, whose sugar acts like added sugar once the fruit's structure is broken, while the sugar in whole fruit, vegetables and milk is left out.

Sugar hides under other names, at least 56 by one count and 61 by another: molasses, cane juice, agave nectar, corn syrup, dextrose and maltose are all sugar, so a cereal can be loaded with it though the word sugar never appears. A handy clue is the ending -ose, as in dextrose, fructose, maltose, lactose and sucrose, which almost always flags a sugar, though honey, agave, cane juice, molasses and plain syrup carry no -ose and slip past the trick.

Corn syrup is mostly glucose and only mildly sweet, so factories add an enzyme that rearranges part of the glucose into fructose, which tastes sweeter; the result, high-fructose corn syrup, is about as sweet as table sugar, itself half glucose and half fructose. American soda makers switched to it partly on price, since tariffs and quotas kept imported cane sugar dear while corn was subsidised, and partly because a liquid pours: it could be pumped straight into the mix instead of shovelled and dissolved like granulated sugar.

The WHO's ideal limit for added sugar is about six teaspoons a day, yet a single standard can of Coca-Cola, 12 ounces, holds about 39 grams, roughly ten teaspoons, which blows past the whole day's budget in a single drink.

Ingredient lists run from the most to the least, so a maker whose product is mostly sugar can divide the sugar among several different names, corn syrup third, high-fructose corn syrup seventh and dextrose tenth, so that no single sugar tops the list though together they are the main ingredient.

Scientists still argue about sugar. Robert Lustig, an American doctor, argues that it is a unique poison for the liver, while others answer that it is simply empty calories, no worse than any treat eaten in excess. Two harms, though, are not seriously disputed: sugar feeds the bacteria that rot teeth into cavities, and it makes extra calories easy to pile on. Skeptics of the poison story point out that nobody has found the amount at which sugar stops being a treat and becomes a toxin, and they argue that most of its harm comes from the easy extra calories it piles on, which, with too little exercise, can explain much of the rise in obesity. Many researchers settle on a middle reading: sugar clearly drives tooth decay and overeating, so it belongs among treats rather than staples, while the case that it is a unique poison remains unproven.

the-agricultural-revolution-and-the-eigh.context_blurb:
Farming began some eleven thousand years back in the Middle East, when people started sowing wild grasses deliberately rather than just collecting them. A starter kit of eight founder crops, grains, pulses and one plant for cloth, launched settled village life, and farmers elsewhere later invented agriculture all over again with crops of their own.

Farming's birthplace is called the Fertile Crescent, for the moon-shaped arc of land it forms through the Levant and Mesopotamia, from the Mediterranean toward the Persian Gulf, in what are now Iraq, Syria and Jordan; there, roughly 11,500 to 10,000 years ago, the eight founder crops launched agriculture.

Three of the eight were cereal grasses, and two of them, einkorn and emmer, are ancient kinds of wheat, still grown and baked into bread today. Einkorn is the most ancient and primitive of all farmed wheats, and einkorn bread was part of the last meal of Ötzi the Iceman, who lived some fifty-three centuries ago and was found frozen in an Alpine glacier in 1991. The third was barley, the hardiest, able to survive dry spells and salty ground, which is why it travelled farther than either wheat.

Emmer was ancient Egypt's daily bread grain, and its descendants include durum, a hard, glassy wheat that is milled into semolina for pasta. Of the eight founders, one was not grown to eat: flax, raised for the oil pressed from its seeds, linseed, and for the fibres in its stems, spun into linen.

Wild wheat and barley drop their grain as soon as it is ripe, because the stalk that holds it, the rachis, is brittle and snaps. A rare mutant whose seed head held onto its grain was useless in the wild but perfect to harvest, and farmers, without meaning to, selected it until whole fields could be cut at once; that same change means domesticated grain can no longer sow itself without people.

Grain and pulse belong together: cereals are low in the amino acid lysine but rich in methionine, and pulses are the reverse, so eaten together they supply all nine essential amino acids, a complete protein, which is why hummus with pita, dal with rice and beans with rice show up in old food cultures everywhere. The four founding pulses included peas, lentils, chickpeas and one oddity, bitter vetch, whose seeds hold a toxin that can paralyse unless rinsed many times, so it ended up mostly as fodder for farm animals.

Farming was invented more than once: some 9,000 years ago farmers in China's Yangtze valley, with no contact at all, domesticated rice. In Mexico's Balsas River valley, farmers turned teosinte, a scraggly wild grass with a handful of stony kernels, into maize, the corn cob.
