the-andean-potato-and-chuno-freeze-dryin.context_blurb:
The potato is not Irish or European by origin: it began high in the Andes of South America, where farmers still grow thousands of varieties. Andean families also invented a way to make potatoes last for years using nothing but freezing nights, blazing sun and their own feet, while far away in Ireland, total reliance on one cloned potato ended in famine.

The potato was first domesticated 7,000 to 10,000 years ago in the Andes, around Lake Titicaca in what is now southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, and about 3,000 of the world's roughly 5,000 potato varieties still grow there.

To make chuño, families leave potatoes out on nights that freeze to about −5°C, which bursts the potato's cells, and then the strong day sun drives the water out. The chunk left behind is so dry that mould, yeast and bacteria cannot take hold, so it keeps for two to four years and by some accounts a decade. Over about a week the potatoes are frozen at night, thawed and dried by day, and trampled underfoot, traditionally by whole families, to press out the water and slip off the skins until only a small, light chunk remains.

Black chuño is left unwashed, but white chuño, known in Quechua and Aymara as tunta or moraya, is soaked in running water, often a cold stream, before it dries in the sun, which leaves it paler. In Bolivia the hearty soup chairo calls for ground chuño.

Potatoes are grown from cut-up tubers, the seed potatoes, not from true seed, so each plant is a genetic clone of its parent with the same weaknesses. In 1840s Ireland nearly everyone grew a single variety, the Lumper, so when the blight Phytophthora infestans struck, not one plant could resist, and within three years roughly an eighth of Ireland's people were dead.

the-balanced-plate-what-each-part-is-doi.context_blurb:
A simple balanced plate, some protein, some carbohydrate, some fat and a pile of vegetables, is doing more than it seems. Each part has a job the others cannot do, and nutrition scientists have measured how the parts help one another, though the official plate models do not agree on every detail.

Of a dinner of grilled chicken, rice, broccoli with butter and some oil, the grilled chicken is the part that rebuilds you: protein breaks down into about 20 amino acids, the body's building blocks, and proteins such as collagen and keratin form skin, hair, nails, bones and teeth.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble: the body absorbs them only when some fat comes along, so a salad of spinach, carrots and peppers eaten plain leaves much of its vitamin A and K behind, while a little olive oil drizzled over it ferries them in.

Vegetables fill about half the plate on Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate, and they are mostly water and fibre, cucumber about 96 percent water and celery, tomato and zucchini about 95, so a big, filling heap of vegetables carries almost no calories. Oats and white bread carry similar carbohydrates, but oats are rich in soluble fibre, which soaks up water into a thick gel that slows digestion and blunts the blood-sugar surge, so the energy comes slowly instead of all at once.

In a 2005 Ohio State study, adding sliced avocado to a fat-free salad raised the beta-carotene absorbed from its vegetables more than fifteenfold, because the avocado's fat unlocks the vegetables' nutrients.

Harvard's plate refuses to count potatoes as a vegetable, arguing that a plain potato is fast-digested starch that spikes blood sugar much as white bread and sweets do. That is one model's reasoning: the U.S. government's MyPlate still counts the potato as a vegetable, though both guides agree that about half the plate should be produce.

the-basic-cuts-chop-slice-dice-mince.context_blurb:
Chop, slice, dice and mince are not interchangeable words. Each names a particular size and shape of cut, and a good cook learns them because the size of a piece decides how fast it cooks, how it looks and how far its flavour spreads through a dish.

Chopping is the most forgiving cut: rough, bite-sized pieces that need not match in size or shape, which suits a rustic stew whose carrots will simmer for an hour anyway. Dicing is the opposite, all about evenness: the food is cut into neat little cubes of matching size, large, medium or small, so every piece finishes cooking at the same moment.

Mincing is the finest everyday cut, about a sixteenth of an inch, so small the pieces almost melt into the dish, and cooks mince garlic and ginger so a single clove flavours the whole pot. Slicing makes flat, even pieces with a drawing motion, the blade gliding smoothly through the food from tip to heel in one stroke rather than sawing back and forth, which leaves a clean face on a tomato instead of a torn one.

Even cuts matter because, in one hot pan, small pieces cook faster than big ones: toss a pile of uneven onion into sizzling oil and the thin slivers burn before the thick chunks have even cooked through. Uneven pieces ruin a quick sauté or stir-fry, but a rough chop is fine for a vegetable stock, where the vegetables simmer for hours and are then strained out anyway; the rule is to match the cut to the cooking.

Professionals build a dice in three stages: they cut the onion into flat slabs, cut the slabs into sticks, called batonnets, French for little sticks, and then bundle the sticks and cut across them into cubes.

the-berry-paradox-a-banana-is-a-berry-a-.context_blurb:
To a cook, a berry is any small, sweet fruit you can pop in your mouth. Botanists use a stricter rule: a true berry must be a fleshy fruit formed from the single ovary of one flower, with its seeds held within the flesh, and by that rule bananas, grapes and even watermelons are berries while strawberries and raspberries are not.

Among the cherry, the raspberry, the strawberry and the banana, only the banana passes the test: it grows from one flower's single ovary, its whole wall ripens into soft flesh, and its seeds sit inside as the tiny dark specks down its core. Blueberries, cranberries and currants are true berries too, fleshy throughout and grown from one ovary with the seeds inside, while the strawberry, blackberry and raspberry only borrow the word.

The supermarket banana is seedless because it grows and ripens with no fertilisation at all, a trick called parthenocarpy, so its seeds never develop past faint specks, while wild bananas in Southeast Asia are still crammed with seeds hard enough to crack a tooth. The strawberry's sweet red flesh is not its ovary at all but the base the flower sat on, the receptacle, which swells up and turns red, making the strawberry an accessory fruit. The tomato is a true berry, and so are its close cousins in the nightshade family, Solanaceae, the eggplant and the chili pepper; grapes and kiwifruit are berries as well, but from quite different plant families.

The roughly 200 dots on a strawberry's skin, which most people call seeds, are each an achene, a complete little fruit holding a single seed, so those specks are the strawberry's only true fruits. A raspberry crumbles into juicy beads because it is an aggregate fruit: its one flower held many ovaries, and each ripened into a bead called a drupelet, and a blackberry is built the same way. An orange is a berry too, the citrus kind, called a hesperidium, with a leathery, oil-dotted rind and juice-filled segments; lemons and grapefruit are the same.

The avocado is a one-seeded berry: its soft, buttery green flesh is the ripened fruit wall, the ovary, wrapped around one big seed, the pit. Watermelons, cucumbers and pumpkins are pepos, berries of the gourd family with a hard rind that forms from flower tissue fused and hardened over the ovary, which lets a watermelon grow huge without splitting; inside, the flesh has no dividing walls and the seeds lie scattered in the pulp.

A pineapple is a multiple fruit: 50 to 200 separate flowers grew in a spiral and fused as they ripened, each hexagon on its skin marking one former flower. A mulberry forms the same way, so despite its name it is no true berry.

Botany once lost in court. America's Supreme Court ruled in 1893, in Nix v. Hedden, that the tomato, botanically a fruit and even a berry, was a vegetable for the import tax, because, as Justice Horace Gray wrote, it is eaten with dinner, with or after the soup, fish or meat, and not served as dessert as fruits are.

the-bias-cut-why-stir-fry-veg-go-on-the-.context_blurb:
Chinese wok cooks cut their carrots into long, slanted ovals rather than coins. Wok cooks cut them that way on purpose, angling the knife across the vegetable, because in a pan that hot, cooking that fast, the shape of each piece decides how well it cooks.

Tilting the knife to about 30 to 45 degrees and slicing across a carrot, celery stalk or scallion is called cutting on the bias, or on the diagonal, and it turns what would be a round disc into an elongated oval; Japanese cooks call their 45-degree version naname-giri.

The slant gives each slice a much bigger cut face, so the heat of a roaring wok reaches more of each piece at once and it cooks faster and more evenly in its minute or two in the pan, while the extra flat surface also browns faster and soaks up more sauce.

The roll cut, or oblique cut, goes further: slice on the bias, roll the carrot a quarter-turn, slice again and repeat down its length. Because a carrot tapers, a skilled cook opens the knife to a wider slant as she nears the thin tip, so even the narrow end yields a full-size chunk and every piece cooks at the same rate.

the-birth-of-the-restaurant.context_blurb:
Before the late 1700s there was nowhere to sit at your own small table, choose a dish from a list and pay for just that. The restaurant was invented in Paris, born from a bowl of broth, spread by a revolution and crowned more than a century later by a tyre company, and its famous founder may never have existed.

Before restaurants, a traveller at a French inn ate the table d'hôte, the host's table: whatever the innkeeper had cooked, served at his chosen hour, elbow to elbow with strangers at one long table. The first restaurants sold a hearty, steaming meat broth that the French called a restaurant, from the verb restaurer, to restore, because people drank it to rebuild their strength; only later did the word move from the soup to the shop.

Those first restaurants also invented the menu, a list of separate dishes with separate prices, written on a small chalkboard, the carte, since paper was dear and dishes changed daily, and that is why ordering single dishes is still called eating à la carte, by the card. The French Revolution of 1789 spread them: with their noble masters killed or fled, many palace-trained private cooks set up restaurants of their own for the public and served fine food to anyone with coins.

French legend names the first restaurateur Boulanger, a surname that means baker, though the man supposedly sold broth, not bread. The legend says his door bore a Latin motto promising that every sufferer from a sore stomach who came to him would be restored, a cheeky twist on Jesus's welcome in the Gospel of Matthew to all who are weary; like the founder, the sign may be pure legend.

The historian Rebecca Spang searched the Paris archives for him and found no trace that such a man ever lived: no birth record, no shop, not even the lawsuit the legend says he fought. She argues the real pioneer was a promoter named Mathurin Roze de Chantoiseau, around 1766. Spang traced the whole tale to a single late source, a history of French eating printed in 1782 by Le Grand d'Aussy, a former Jesuit, who named an otherwise unknown Boulanger as the inventor in 1765, seventeen years before he wrote.

The most powerful rating in restaurants came from a tyre company: the brothers André and Édouard Michelin made car tyres, and in 1900 they launched their little red guide to send drivers to good restaurants far out in the country, since more driving meant more worn tyres and more sales. About 35,000 free copies went out in 1900, when barely 3,000 cars ran in all of France, and the guide stayed free until 1920, when Michelin began charging seven francs, with André Michelin reportedly declaring that people truly respect only what they pay for. Stars followed, one in 1926 and the three-star scale by the 1930s.

the-braise-boeuf-bourguignon-and-coq-au-.context_blurb:
A braise is slow, wet cooking: meat browned first, then simmered, covered, for hours in liquid until a cheap, tough cut turns tender. Classical French cooking built two of its most famous dishes this way, beef in red Burgundy and rooster in wine, and both carry more myth than most diners realise.

Braising is the way to make a cheap, tough cut meltingly tender: hard-working muscles such as chuck from the shoulder or shank are full of tough connective tissue, and only long, slow, moist cooking turns that toughness silky, the opposite of a fast-grilled steak.

Boeuf bourguignon, beef Burgundy, braises its beef almost entirely in red Burgundy wine, usually with some stock, and that wine gives the dish its deep purple-brown colour and sharp, rich flavour. Coq au vin means rooster in wine: it was born to rescue an old rooster, a mature male bird so full of connective tissue that roasting turned it to shoe leather, by braising it for hours in wine. Both dishes begin the same way: the cook fries lardons, small strips of salt-cured pork, in the empty pot to melt out their fat, browns everything else in that fat and scatters the crisp lardons back near the end.

The tough tissue is collagen, and under hours of moist, gentle heat, starting around 70°C and finishing near a simmer, it unravels and melts into gelatin, the silky, lip-coating substance that gives the sauce its body; dry heat alone cannot do it. Searing the meat deep brown in a hot, dry pan before any liquid goes in builds a crust full of brand-new savoury flavours through the Maillard reaction, in which amino acids and sugars form hundreds of new compounds. It happens only on a dry surface, because meat sitting in wine cannot rise above boiling, and it does not seal in juices, as the old myth claims.

The dark, browned layer left stuck to the pot after searing is the fond, French for base, and when the wine is poured in and scraped across it, a step called deglazing, that layer melts into the sauce as its savoury backbone. The wine does not really tenderise the beef, which is the slow, moist heat's job; simmering uncovered, the wine reduces, its water boiling off until it concentrates into a thick, glossy, deeply flavoured sauce. Some sources still credit its acidity with a small tenderising role.

Boeuf bourguignon is not an ancient peasant recipe: it was first written down in 1867 and belonged to the bistros of Paris, called a Burgundian specialty only in the 20th century, so the Burgundy in its name points to the wine, not an old home. Coq au vin's legend says it dates to Julius Caesar's war with the Gauls, when a defiant chief sent Caesar a scrawny rooster as an insult, but no written recipe for the dish appears until the early 1900s, so historians call the tale a story. Julia Child later brought coq au vin to American kitchens.

the-buffet-and-the-smorgasbord.context_blurb:
Swedish hosts let guests fetch their own food: it waits down one long table and every guest serves himself. Swedes call that spread the smörgåsbord, English took up the name for any big, varied help-yourself spread, and it grew from a small pre-dinner table of bread, cheese and schnapps.

Word for word, smörgåsbord means the sandwich table, because a smörgås is an open-faced buttered-bread sandwich and a bord is a table. English borrowed the word in 1893 and has used it for any huge medley since 1948.

A smörgåsbord runs in a strict order, with a fresh plate for every round: it opens with pickled herring, sill, on a clean plate of its own so its strong tang cannot bleed into what follows, then cold fish, cold meats, warm dishes and cheese, and hot and cold food never share a plate.

Its ancestor, dating to the 1500s, was the brännvinsbord, the schnapps table, with bread, cheese and butter laid out beside aquavit, which merchant families served as an appetiser, eaten standing, sometimes two to five hours before the real dinner. Over the centuries it swelled into the full smörgåsbord, whose grandest form is the julbord, the Christmas table.

the-catherine-de-medici-myth.context_blurb:
A famous story says French cooking began in 1533, when the fourteen-year-old Catherine de' Medici of Florence married into the French royal family and brought Italian cooks with her. Cookbooks repeated it for centuries, but food historians call it a fairy tale that grew in the telling.

Over the years the legend piled one trophy after another into her luggage, artichokes, sorbet, olive oil, truffles and even the fork, which the tale falsely credits her with bringing to French tables, though no early record supports any of it.

French cooking truly changed course in 1651, over a hundred years after that wedding, when the French chef François Pierre de La Varenne wrote the first true French cookbook, Le Cuisinier françois, replacing the old, heavily spiced dishes and teaching roux, béchamel, stocks and butter in place of lard, none of it Italian.

The historian Susan Pinkard, in A Revolution in Taste, set the menus of rich Florentines in the 1530s beside the dishes of the French court and found the two essentially identical, because elite Renaissance kitchens across Europe shared one complex, spicy, sweet style. There was no separate French cuisine for an Italian bride to create.

the-chemistry-set-label-what-ultra-proce.context_blurb:
Ultra-processed food is a label for products built in factories from industrial ingredients, starches, sugars and oils pulled out of whole foods, plus additives such as emulsifiers, flavourings and colourings, rather than from foods a home cook would recognise. Researchers sort foods by how processed they are, and a growing body of research links ultra-processed food to poorer health, though scientists still argue over why.

Ultra-processed foods are everyday things, soft drinks, packaged snacks, chicken nuggets, sweetened cereals, mass-produced bread, ice cream and instant noodles, and a brick of instant ramen, refined-flour noodles plus a seasoning packet, is a factory product from start to finish. A handy rule of thumb is to read the ingredient list: the more ingredients you cannot picture as real food, especially five or more of them, the more processed the product is likely to be.

NOVA, a ranking that Carlos Monteiro, a Brazilian nutrition scientist at the University of São Paulo, created in 2009, ignores fat, sugar and salt entirely and judges only processing. So butter, which is almost entirely fat, sits in its second-mildest group, while vanilla ice cream from the supermarket lands in the most processed, because besides cream and sugar it holds emulsifiers, stabilisers and flavourings no home kitchen stocks. Group 1 is whole or minimally processed food such as fruit, vegetables, eggs, meat and milk, and milk that has been pasteurised and cartoned stays in Group 1 because nothing has been added to it. Group 2 holds kitchen ingredients drawn from whole foods, such as butter, oil, sugar and salt, Group 3 combines the two, like cheese or fresh bread, and Group 4 is ultra-processed.

The line can fall between two loaves on the same shelf: a bakery loaf of flour, water, salt and yeast is plain processed food, Group 3, while a soft, sliced supermarket loaf is ultra-processed because it contains emulsifiers and preservatives that no home baker would add.

Big surveys tie heavy ultra-processed eating to more obesity, diabetes and heart disease, but careful scientists note that a survey shows only a link, not proof of cause, and the real culprit might simply be extra calories from energy-dense food, or ultra-processed food crowding whole foods off the plate, rather than the processing itself.

In a month-long study at America's National Institutes of Health, 20 volunteers ate a fortnight of ultra-processed meals and a fortnight of whole-food meals, the two menus matched nutrient for nutrient, and they gained about 0.9 kilograms, two pounds, on the ultra-processed food and lost about the same on the whole food.

the-chili-family-jalapeno-to-chipotle-sc.context_blurb:
Jalapeño, poblano, habanero, chipotle: Mexico's chilies are a huge family, bred, dried and smoked into dozens of flavours and heats. Their story runs from wild plants of the Americas to kitchens around the world, and from a pharmacist's tasting panel to a Nobel Prize for explaining the burn.

A chili's burn is not real heat and not a taste at all: a thermometer on your tongue would not rise a degree, because capsaicin, the chili's fiery chemical, tricks your pain nerves into sounding an alarm. The fire is not in the seeds either: about 85 percent of the capsaicin sits in the pale, spongy ribs, the placenta, that the seeds cling to, so scraping out only the seeds barely cools a chili, while cutting out the ribs does.

Capsaicin is oily and will not dissolve in water, so a gulp of water just spreads it around the mouth, while a glass of milk carries it away and cools the burn. Milk works because of casein, a protein that acts like a detergent and grabs the oily capsaicin off the nerve endings; in tests skim milk cooled the burn as well as whole milk, so the protein, not the fat, does the job.

A chipotle, with its deep, smoky, almost meaty flavour, is simply a jalapeño smoked and dried over wood; lightly smoked ones are called moritas and heavily smoked ones mecos. Drying renames chilies too: a fresh green poblano, dried to a wrinkled, dark, sweetly raisin-like pod, becomes an ancho, just as a dried mirasol becomes a guajillo.

The Scoville scale ranks chilies by heat: a jalapeño scores about 2,500 to 8,000 units, while a habanero runs 100,000 to 350,000, dozens of times hotter. Since October 2023 the hottest chili on record has been Pepper X, at about 2.7 million units by Guinness's count, well ahead of the 1.64 million of the Carolina Reaper it replaced; both came from the same South Carolina breeder, Ed Currie, and his Puckerbutt Pepper Company.

The scale was invented in 1912 by the pharmacist Wilbur Scoville, who diluted a pepper in sugar water until a panel of tasters could no longer feel the burn, and how much sugar water it took became the score; on that ladder a bell pepper reads zero and pure capsaicin about 16 million.

Every chili on Earth traces back to the Americas: the wild Capsicum plants came from the Peru and Bolivia region and were first domesticated in Mexico about 6,000 years ago. There were no chilies in India, Thailand, Sichuan, Hungary or Korea until Spanish and Portuguese ships spread them after Columbus reached the New World in 1492. Kimchi is centuries older than its chili: before chilies reached Korea, around 1600, it was a pale, salt-brined pickle of radish and other vegetables; chili first appears in kimchi recipes around 1700, and fiery red kimchi became common only in the 1800s.

The 2021 Nobel Prize in Medicine went to David Julius for showing how the burn works: capsaicin switches on TRPV1, the nerve sensor whose everyday job is sensing genuine heat, firing at scalding temperatures above about 43°C, so the brain reads a chili as a real burn.

Why would a plant make its fruit burn? The directed-deterrence idea holds that capsaicin evolved to keep away mammals, whose grinding teeth destroy the seeds, while birds feel no burn and swallow the fruit whole, spreading the seeds. The ecologist Joshua Tewksbury filmed wild chilies and found only birds ate them in daylight, and showed that capsaicin also fights the fungus that rots seeds.

the-columbian-exchange-how-chili-conquer.context_blurb:
Chili heat now runs through the cooking of India, Korea and Hungary, yet five hundred years ago nobody outside the Americas had ever tasted a chili. After Columbus, European ships carried the plant around the globe, and within a few generations it had conquered cuisines that now seem unthinkable without it.

Every chili descends from Capsicum, a plant native to the Americas and unknown in Europe, Asia and Africa until Columbus's voyages reached the New World in 1492. So a feast at an Asian royal court around 1300 had no chili heat at all, because no chili had yet arrived anywhere in Asia; the fire of Thai curry, Indian vindaloo, Korean kimchi and Sichuan hot pot is less than about 500 years old.

Portuguese traders spread it fast, carrying chilies around the Cape of Good Hope to their colony at Goa early in the 1500s, while Spanish galleons carried them across the Pacific to the Philippines, and within about a century chili had spread across Africa, India, Southeast Asia, China, Korea and Japan.

Hungary's beloved paprika, the rosy-red powder dusted over goulash, is simply sweet red chili peppers dried and ground, and chilies had reached the Balkans by 1569, so even Hungarian paprika is post-Columbian. Kimchi was a pale, white pickle, often of radish, for most of its history. Chilies reached Korea around 1600, first recorded in the encyclopedia Jibong Yuseol of 1614; about a century later they began to turn up in kimchi, and the red, spicy kimchi people picture today became common only in the 1800s.

The burn fools the body: spicy is not one of the tongue's five tastes, and capsaicin binds TRPV1, the same nerve sensor that detects real burning heat, so the mouth feels a fire that is not there. Water cannot help, because capsaicin is oily and will not dissolve in it, so a gulp only spreads the fire, while milk's protein, casein, surrounds the oily capsaicin and lifts it off the pain receptors, rinsing it away.

The burn is a defence: mammals' grinding molars crush chili seeds, so capsaicin drives mammals away, while birds lack the sensitive receptor, feel no heat and scatter the seeds unharmed in their droppings. The chili's conquest of human kitchens was an accident of that defence.

Sichuan hot pot pairs two jolts, la, the burn of the imported chili, and ma, a buzzing, numbing tingle that came first: it comes from Sichuan pepper, which is neither chili nor pepper but the fruit of a prickly-ash tree, a relative of citrus, whose numbing compound is hydroxy-alpha-sanshool.

the-complete-protein-all-nine-blocks-in-.context_blurb:
Your body builds its proteins from about twenty amino acids, and nine of them it cannot make for itself, so they must come from food. A food that supplies all nine in one serving is called a complete protein, and both the foods that are complete and the plant pairings that become complete together follow a clear pattern.

The nine essential amino acids, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine, must come from food, and meat, fish and eggs, along with milk, reliably carry all nine at once, because the animal already assembled every one in its own body.

Rice and beans, a cheap staple of the Caribbean, West Africa and Latin America, are complete together though neither is alone: rice is low in lysine but rich in methionine, beans the reverse, so each patches the other's gap, a trick called protein complementing. Milk's main protein, casein, is the one that curdles into cheese curds, and its name comes from the Latin caseus, cheese, the same root as the Spanish queso.

Scientists rate every protein against a whole egg, whose biological value is fixed at 100, because an egg must hold everything needed to build a chick, so its nine amino acids come in nearly ideal balance. The scale goes back to H. H. Mitchell in 1923, and whey and milk score close to the egg, but it remains the yardstick.

Frances Moore Lappé's 1971 bestseller, Diet for a Small Planet, urged vegetarians to pair plant proteins at every meal, but in the 1981 tenth-anniversary edition she reversed herself, writing that it was much easier than she had thought, since the body pools amino acids over a whole day. Complementing still works, just not plate by plate.

the-cooking-pot-how-boiling-changed-the-.context_blurb:
The oldest cooking pots ever found, clay vessels about 20,000 years old, were found in a southern Chinese cave called Xianrendong. A pot that could stand in the flames changed the human menu, letting cooks boil, stew and simmer, though people had found a clumsier way to boil long before.

The Xianrendong potters were roaming hunter-gatherers, foraging through the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age about ten thousand years before farming reached the region, so pottery did not need agriculture at all. Many of the fragments carry soot and scorch marks up their outer walls, the sign that a pot sat right in a fire, so these were cooking pots, not only storage jars.

The archaeologist Zhijun Zhao thinks the pots had many uses, including boiling clams and snails, food you cannot really roast but that steams open in a bubbling pot.

Boiling itself is older still, about 30,000 years: before pots, people heated stones in the fire and dropped them into skin bags, bark baskets or hide-lined pits until the water boiled, since the bag itself would burn on the flames. The pot made boiling easy, because it could go straight onto the fire. Ice Age hunters wasted nothing: after cracking long bones for marrow, they smashed the spongy bone ends and boiled the pieces for hours, and the fat melted and rose to the surface as bone grease, which they skimmed off and kept as a calorie-dense food that stored and travelled well.

Raw acorns are too bitter to eat because of tannins, the astringent compounds that pucker the mouth in strong tea, yet acorns were long a staple food in Native California. Tannins dissolve in water, so cooks soaked chopped acorns in change after change of water to wash them out; cold water takes days, but three or four changes of boiling water do it in under an hour. A pot can wash a poison out.

the-cookware-line-up-each-pans-job.context_blurb:
A cook's pans are not interchangeable. Each metal stores and spreads heat in its own way, reacts with food or refuses to, and needs its own care, so a working kitchen keeps a small team of pans and gives each one the job it does best.

For delicate eggs, reach for a nonstick skillet: its slick coating, a plastic called PTFE and sold as Teflon, gives the egg nothing to grip, so a soft French omelette slides and rolls instead of tearing. Nothing browns on it either, so it is no pan for a sear.

For a sear, cooks want cast iron. Thick and heavy, cast iron banks a huge reserve of heat, roughly three times what a comparable stainless pan holds, so a cold steak dropped onto it barely cools the metal. On thin stainless the surface can crash by 150 to 200°F and the meat steams grey; on cast iron the drop is usually under 50°F, and the steak keeps browning.

Bare iron has one weakness, acid: a long tomato simmer or a wine sauce can react with bare iron, aluminum or copper and pick up a dull, metallic taste, but stainless steel is non-reactive, so acidic dishes come out of it clean and bright.

Nonstick has a limit of its own. Left empty on a high burner, a nonstick pan can pass 500°F in two or three minutes, and above about 570°F its coating breaks down and gives off fumes. A person who breathes them gets chills and a headache, nicknamed Teflon flu, but the same fumes kill pet birds quickly.

Stainless steel hides a flaw too. On its own it carries heat poorly, worse than almost any other common pan metal, and a plain stainless pan cooks in hot spots and cold patches. So good stainless pans are clad: a core of aluminum or copper is sealed between the steel layers, and that hidden metal spreads the heat evenly across the whole base.

The slick black skin on an old cast iron skillet is called seasoning, and it is oil, wiped on thin and baked hard, coat after coat, until it sets into a tough film. That film is both the pan's nonstick surface and the shield that keeps bare iron from rusting.

The chemistry happens in the oven. A cook wipes on a very thin coat of oil and bakes the pan hot for about an hour, past the oil's smoke point. There the oil polymerizes: its fat molecules break apart, and the heat links the small, reactive pieces to one another until they form one big solid network bonded to the metal. Some of the oil even reacts with the iron's surface to form a compound that glues the film in place, so true seasoning shrugs off soap.

the-cornish-pasty.context_blurb:
The Cornish pasty is the hand pie of Cornwall, at England's rocky south-western tip, and for generations it was the packed lunch of the tin miners. A miner worked too deep to climb out at midday, so his wife baked him a whole meal sealed in pastry that fit in a pocket and kept him warm.

Inside go chunks of beef, potato, onion and swede, the yellow root Americans call rutabaga, and every one of them goes in raw. Sealed in shortcrust and baked, the filling cooks in its own steam while the meat juices and onion become a rich gravy.

Along one edge runs a fat, crimped rope of pastry, and tradition gives it a job. A miner's hands were black with ore dust that could carry arsenic. So, the story goes, he held his pasty by that thick crust like a handle and threw the crust away when he finished. Historians doubt the tale: the earliest Cornish pasty recipe book, from 1929, says pasties were carried in paper or muslin bags and eaten end to end, and food was too precious to waste.

Since 2011 the name has been protected by European law. A real Cornish pasty must be made in Cornwall, shaped like a D, filled with chunky raw meat and vegetables, and crimped along its side. A baker who seals the pastry over the top instead of down one side may not sell his pie as a Cornish pasty, however perfect the filling.

the-creaming-method-beating-butter-and-s.context_blurb:
Almost every butter cake and cookie begins the same way. Softened butter and sugar go into a bowl and are beaten, by spoon or mixer, for several solid minutes before a single egg or spoonful of flour joins them. Bakers call this creaming, and it builds a cake's lightness long before the oven is switched on.

Creaming is not simply stirring two things together: the beating whips thousands of tiny air bubbles down into the solid fat, and light and fluffy is just what butter looks like once it is full of air. You can watch it happen, because done well the mix nearly doubles in volume and fades from a bright buttery yellow to pale ivory.

The sugar is the hidden worker. Its hard, jagged crystals act like tiny shovels, digging little pockets of air into the soft butter on every turn of the beater. Beat butter alone and it hardly fluffs at all, because in this step sugar is the aerator, not the sweetener.

Those pockets matter because nothing later can make new ones. Baking powder, baking soda, steam and yeast create no bubbles of their own; each can only inflate the pockets already whipped into the batter. So a baker who rushes the creaming and tips in extra powder to rescue the rise still gets a dense, heavy cake, with too few pockets there to blow up.

Temperature matters as much as time. Let the butter grow warm, past about 68°F, and its fat gives way and lets the creamed-in air escape, and that breakdown is permanent: chilling the butter solid again will not bring the air back. With the air gone, cookies spread thin and greasy and cakes bake flat, which is why recipes insist on butter that is softened, never melted.

Bakers in the 1700s had no chemical leaveners at all, so they raised their cakes on creaming alone, beating for ten long minutes. The most famous of these cakes is pound cake, named, as the story goes, because it called for a pound each of flour, butter, sugar and eggs, a recipe simple enough to carry in your head at a time when plenty of cooks could not read.

Even the size of the sugar crystals shows in the crumb. Superfine caster sugar has far more crystals than ordinary granulated sugar, each one much smaller, so it cuts more air pockets, and smaller ones, into the butter, and the cake bakes taller, lighter and finer. Coarse sugar cuts fewer, larger pockets and bakes denser.

the-cutting-board-wood-plastic-and-the-b.context_blurb:
For decades cooks argued over which cutting board was safer: smooth plastic, which looks easy to clean, or wood, which looks porous and full of hiding places. A food scientist in California put the question to an experiment, and the answer surprised him as much as anyone.

Whatever the board, the first rule is the same. Juices from raw chicken may carry salmonella, and a tomato salad is eaten raw, so nothing will ever kill what the board hands over. Food-safety experts say raw meat and ready-to-eat food belong on separate boards, so the tomatoes get a fresh board of their own, or at the very least one scrubbed clean after the chicken.

Wood needs one more kind of care, because it is thirsty. Left soaking in the sink or sent through a dishwasher's long, hot cycle, a wooden board soaks up water and swells, then cracks and warps out of shape. Those splits are permanent, and they are real hiding places for germs, so a wooden board is washed quickly in warm soapy water and dried straight away.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the USDA urged home cooks to throw out wooden boards and switch to plastic. Dean Cliver, a food microbiologist at UC Davis, went looking for the research behind that advice and found there was none: no study had ever shown plastic to be safer, and the agency admitted it. Cliver set out to show how wood could be made as safe as plastic, and his data turned on him.

He spread disease bacteria on wooden boards and, within minutes, could not recover them, because the porous grain had pulled them down inside, where, he wrote, they do not multiply and gradually die. Plastic aged worse. A new plastic board wipes clean, but every knife stroke carves shallow grooves into it, and those grooves hold bacteria right at the surface where the next food will land. Cliver found scarred plastic all but impossible to clean by hand, and used plastic gave back more live bacteria than used wood.

Cliver was careful not to oversell. Germs trapped in the grain are not killed instantly, but nobody has ever shown a knife dragging them back up to the surface. A wooden board is never sterile, which is why separate boards and washing still matter.

The toughest board of all is the butcher's end-grain block, built from short blocks of hardwood stood on their ends like a bundle of straws. The blade slips down between the upright fibres, which part to let it in and then spring back together, so the cut marks close up and the knife's edge stays sharp longer. Cooks call it self-healing, though nothing grows: the fibres are simply pushed aside and return.

To keep any wooden board sealed against water, rub it now and then with food-grade mineral oil, a clear, inert petroleum oil that never spoils. Cooking oils from plants and seeds, such as olive or vegetable oil, are the wrong choice, because once they soak into the grain they go rancid and leave the board smelling foul.

the-danger-zone-40-140-f.context_blurb:
Between the cold of a refrigerator and the heat of a cooking pot lies a band of warmth, from about 40°F up to 140°F. Food scientists call it the danger zone, because in that range the bacteria behind food poisoning, such as Salmonella and Staph, multiply faster than anywhere else. Almost every rule about cooling, holding and reheating food exists to keep meals out of it.

Food in the danger zone can look and smell perfectly fine, so the rule runs on the clock instead. Perishable food should sit out of the fridge for no more than about 2 hours, and only one hour on a day hotter than 90°F; after that, the potato salad forgotten at a party belongs in the bin.

The clock is short because bacteria multiply by splitting: each cell divides into two, and in the danger zone that can happen about every 20 minutes. Doubling stacks up fast. One cell becomes 8 in an hour, 64 in two, and more than two million in about seven hours.

Not every point in the zone is equally dangerous. A germ like Staph grows across a wide stretch of it but breeds fastest right around human body temperature, about 98°F, which makes a warm room a perfect incubator for the bacteria people shed onto food. Staph poisoning also strikes fast, with nausea and cramps usually beginning within a few hours of the meal.

Leftovers need real heat to be safe again: a reheated plate should reach 165°F at its centre, checked with a food thermometer, and soups and gravies should come to a rolling boil.

For anyone feeding a crowd, the whole science comes down to one rule: keep the hot food hot, and the cold food cold. Hot dishes are held at 140°F or above in chafing dishes or on steam tables, cold ones sit nested in ice at 40°F or below, and nothing is allowed to drift into the middle.

The real trouble is the trip through the zone. A slow cooker is a poor way to warm up cold stew, because it heats food so gently that the stew lingers for hours in the danger zone on its way up; the stove, oven or microwave gets it through fast. Cooling has the same problem in reverse. A deep pot of chili put straight into the fridge chills at its edges while its packed centre holds its heat for hours, so leftovers should be divided into several shallow containers that cool all the way through quickly.

Heat has one last limit. Reheating kills living bacteria, but some germs that grow in food left out, Staph among them, have already left behind a toxin that heat cannot destroy, a poison that survives even an hour or two at a rolling boil. Rice left on the stove all afternoon, the kind behind the outbreaks of Bacillus cereus that doctors nickname fried rice syndrome, cannot be rescued by microwaving it piping hot: the germs may die, but their toxin stays.

the-fig-is-a-flower-turned-outside-in.context_blurb:
A ripe fig sits in the fruit bowl like any other fruit, purple-skinned and honey-sweet. Botanists see something far stranger: a hollow pod turned outside-in, a hidden garden sealed in the dark, and a partnership with a tiny insect that ranks among the oddest bargains in nature.

The soft fig is really a whole bunch of tiny flowers, hundreds of them, lining the inside of a fleshy, hollow pod that botanists call a syconium, so the blooms face inward where no one ever sees them. Once pollinated, each of those flowers becomes a minute fruit of its own, so the crunchy specks between your teeth are not simply seeds but a crowd of separate little fruits packed together.

Flowers sealed in the dark pose a puzzle, because no bee can ever reach them. The fig is pollinated from within, by a tiny fig wasp that squeezes in through a pinhole at the fig's tip, called the ostiole, which opens only for a short time when the fig is ready.

Each species of fig is matched to one species of wasp, and a ready fig gives off a scent that draws only the female of that one species, guiding her to the hole while other insects pass it by. Neither partner can reproduce without the other.

The way in is brutally tight, so tight that pushing through rips off the female's wings and bits of her antennae. It is a one-way trip. Inside she pollinates the flowers, lays her eggs and dies.

Yet nobody finds a wasp in a ripe fig, because the fig makes an enzyme, ficin, that digests the dead wasp's body and soaks her nutrients into the ripening fruit. The fig has, in effect, eaten her.

Most figs sold in shops never needed a wasp at all: varieties such as Black Mission, Brown Turkey and Kadota were bred to swell and ripen with no pollination whatsoever, so their fruit grows plump and sweet without a single visitor.

the-first-bread-before-farming-natufian-.context_blurb:
About 14,400 years ago, at a camp called Shubayqa 1 in the Black Desert of north-eastern Jordan, someone baked bread beside an open fire. Archaeologists dug the charred crumbs, only millimetres across, out of two stacked fireplaces, and they are the oldest bread anyone has found. The find turned an old story about bread's beginnings upside down.

The bakers were Natufians, hunter-gatherers of the ancient Levant who grew no crops at all: their bread is some 4,000 years older than the first farms. They gathered wild wheat and barley and crushed the grain into a coarse flour on flat grinding stones.

Their bread never rose, because the Natufians had no yeast, so the dough baked flat and hard like a cracker. The crumbs closely match the unleavened flatbreads of much later times; loaves raised with yeast came thousands of years afterward.

The plant scientist who led the analysis, Amaia Arranz-Otaegui of the University of Copenhagen, baked her own copy of the recipe from wild grains and tasted it, and she judged the result salty overall and a little gritty, the grit coming partly from grain ground on rough stone. Cooking an ancient recipe to learn from it is called experimental archaeology.

The flour was not all grain: the bakers pounded in the starchy underground tubers of club-rush, a reed-like plant of wet, marshy ground, so each flatbread was part cereal and part ground-up marsh root.

No oven has ever turned up at the site, because the Natufians did not need one: they worked the flour with water into a stiff dough and baked it right in the hot ashes and embers of the hearth.

All that grinding, sieving and kneading made each small flatbread hard-won. The researchers have suggested that the wish to make more of this special food may have been one of the forces that pushed people to invent farming itself, though that idea is a hypothesis, not a settled fact. If they are right, the bread came first and the farm followed.

the-fishmongers-freshness-test.context_blurb:
At a good fish counter the fish lie whole on crushed ice, and a fishmonger can read each one's age like a clock. Nose, eyes, flesh and gills each give a clue to how long ago the fish left the water, and the smells behind those clues come from some surprising chemistry.

Start with the nose: a truly fresh fish smells of almost nothing but the clean, open sea and a little brine or seaweed, and even a faint note of cucumber or hay means it is no longer perfectly fresh. A strong fishy reek is the sign that a fish is past its best.

Then the eyes, which change early: a fresh fish looks back at you with clear, plump, and bulging eyes that shine like metal, while dull, cloudy or sunken eyes mean it has been lying around.

Press a fingertip into the flesh behind the head, and fresh muscle springs right back like your own skin; a dent that stays means the flesh has begun to break down.

If you can check only one thing, check the gills, which the fish scientists at Nofima, Norway's big food-research institute, rank as the most reliable sign of all: bright red or pink means a recent catch, while brown, grey or green means the fish is no longer fresh.

The fishy smell has a story of its own. A saltwater fish keeps an odourless compound, TMAO, in its flesh to stop its cells shrivelling in the salty sea. After death, bacteria break that compound down into a smellier relative, TMA, and that one molecule makes up about 95 per cent of what people call fishy smell. The reek is the sign of bacteria at work, not of the fish itself.

That explains the lemon wedge: TMA is light enough to float up from the plate to your nose, but lemon's acid hands it a proton and locks it into a heavy salt that stays dissolved in the juice and cannot rise. The smell is not masked; it is pinned down.

Freshwater fish carry little TMAO, yet a farm-pond catfish or trout can taste muddy even on the day it is caught. The earthy note is geosmin, made by microbes living in the pond or lake water and soaked up through the fish's gills, so it is a taste of the place the fish swam, not of spoilage. It is the same molecule that gives rain on dry soil and raw beets their earthy smell.

Sharks, skates and rays balance the salty sea another way, by storing urea, the same waste our own bodies flush out in urine, in their flesh. After death the urea breaks down into ammonia, so a skate wing can smell like a cleaning cupboard without being spoiled at all; in fact skate is better after a day or two, once the flesh has softened.

the-five-basic-tastes-and-the-tongue-map.context_blurb:
Your tongue reads five basic tastes, sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, and each one carries a chemical message about food: energy, minerals, spoilage, poison or protein. Yet much of what people learned about taste at school was wrong, starting with a famous map, and some of what we call taste is not taste at all.

The old textbook tongue map, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back, is a myth: every basic taste is picked up all over the tongue. The map grew from a 1901 German paper that found only tiny differences in sensitivity from place to place; later writers inflated those small bumps into hard zones, and a 1974 re-test by Virginia Collings confirmed that every taste is felt everywhere.

The tongue also gets credit it has not earned. On its own it can tell you only that a strawberry is sweet and a little sour. The rich strawberry flavour comes from smell: aroma molecules drift up the back of the throat into the nose, and that route supplies something like 80 to 90 per cent of what we call flavour. Pinch your nose while eating a jelly bean and you taste only sweetness; let go, and cherry or lemon suddenly appears.

Each basic taste has its own trigger. Sour is the tongue sensing acid, the hydrogen ions that pour off acidic foods, which is why a lemon, a spoonful of vinegar and a sour sweet all make the same pucker. Salty works through a gateway on the tongue that opens only for sodium, so salt substitutes made with potassium do not fit it and taste metallic or bitter instead of cleanly salty.

The fifth taste was found in a bowl of kelp broth: in 1908 the Tokyo chemist Kikunae Ikeda was eating kombu dashi, the classic Japanese stock, and noticed a savoury depth the other four tastes could not explain. He isolated glutamate from the kelp, named the taste umami, from the Japanese for delicious, and patented a way to make its salt, MSG.

Bitter is the body's poison alarm, and because natural poisons come in countless chemical shapes, the tongue carries about 25 kinds of bitter detector to catch them all, far more than for any other taste. The alarm is deliberately touchy, which is one reason many children push away bitter greens.

Burn your tongue on hot pizza and the dullness lasts only days, because taste cells are replaced constantly: each lives only about ten days to two weeks before new ones grow from stem cells in the taste bud.

Some sensations only pretend to be tastes. The burn of chilli and the chill of mint are touch and temperature sensations, carried by the nerves that feel heat, cold and pain in your skin, not by the taste buds at all. Chilli's capsaicin trips the same sensor that warns of burning heat, and mint's menthol trips the cold sensor.

Soda's fizzy bite, on the other hand, is partly a real taste: an enzyme on the tongue's sour cells turns dissolved carbon dioxide into acid, so carbonation is read as a sharp touch of sour, not just bubbles popping. In a pressure chamber where no bubbles can burst, the fizz feels the same.

the-five-leaveners-what-makes-it-rise.context_blurb:
A puffy loaf, a tall cake, a hollow cream puff: each one rises because gas gets trapped inside it and pushes outward. Bakers have five ways to make that gas, called leaveners: living yeast, baking soda, baking powder, steam and plain air, and every recipe picks the one that gives the texture it wants.

The oldest leavener is alive: baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus that eats the sugars in dough and breathes out carbon dioxide, and the stretchy gluten in the dough traps those bubbles so the loaf swells. Bread rises because a living thing is feeding inside it.

Chemical leaveners came much later. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and on its own it is almost useless. It fizzes out carbon dioxide only when it meets an acid, a sour partner such as buttermilk, yogurt, lemon juice or natural cocoa, which is why every recipe raised with soda hides something sour.

Baking powder solves that problem by carrying its own partner: it is baking soda with a dry acid, classically cream of tartar, already blended in, so it works with plain milk or water. A sealed can can sit for months and never go flat thanks to a third ingredient, cornstarch, which soaks up stray moisture and keeps the acid and the soda from reacting early.

Most powder today is double-acting: it releases a first fizz when the batter gets wet and saves a second, bigger burst for when oven heat reaches it. That second burst is a safety net, so a batter left waiting for twenty minutes still bakes up tall, where the old single-acting powder would have spent all its gas on the counter.

Cream of tartar has a surprising birthplace, because it is a by-product of winemaking. As grape juice ferments, the acid crystallises into a gritty crust on the inside of the wine barrels, called wine stone, and that crust is scraped off and purified into the white powder.

Some pastries need no chemical help at all. Choux pastry, the dough of cream puffs and éclairs, is so wet that in a hot oven its water flashes into steam, and the pressure blows each puff into a hollow shell ready to be filled. Angel food cake rises on air alone: the baker whips air into a dozen egg whites, and the egg-white proteins unfold and wrap each tiny bubble to hold it, so the leavener, bakers like to say, is the whisk.

Acid and alkali matter even in the cocoa tin. Dutch-processed cocoa has been treated with an alkali to tame its natural acidity, so it can no longer set baking soda fizzing. Natural cocoa is acidic and pairs with soda; switch to Dutch cocoa and the recipe must switch to baking powder, which brings its own acid.

the-five-mother-sauces.context_blurb:
Behind almost every classic French sauce stands one of five mother sauces, bases a cook learns first and then varies into hundreds of children. The great chef Auguste Escoffier fixed the list of five in 1903, and knowing them means knowing how a French cook thinks: choose a thickener, choose a liquid, then add the flavour.

The thickener under most of them is a roux, a paste of flour and fat in equal weights, cooked together in the pan before any liquid goes in. Whatever liquid then loosens the roux decides which sauce you end up with.

Loosen a pale roux with milk and you have the simplest of the five, béchamel, the creamy white sauce layered through lasagne and binding the cheese in macaroni. It is named after Louis de Béchameil, a steward to King Louis XIV, who almost certainly never invented it; a rival courtier grumbled that he had served creamed chicken before Béchameil was born and never got a sauce named after him.

Loosen a barely cooked, blond roux with a pale stock of unroasted chicken, veal or fish bones instead, and you get velouté, French for velvety, always named for the stock inside it: a chicken velouté, a fish velouté.

For the darkest of the five, espagnole, the cook roasts beef or veal bones deep brown for the stock and cooks the roux dark and nutty, and those two browned ingredients give the sauce its colour. Its name means Spanish, though the sauce is French; a legend credits Spanish cooks who came to court with Queen Anne of Austria, but no record puts them in the royal kitchens.

One mother needs no roux at all: sauce tomate thickens itself as the tomatoes cook down and their water boils away. No medieval French cook could have made it, because the tomato is a crop of the Americas that reached Europe only in the 1500s, and the oldest tomato-sauce recipe that survives dates from Naples in 1692.

Hollandaise skips both the roux and the long simmer: warm egg yolks are whisked with melted butter until the yolks hold it in a thick, glossy emulsion, sharpened with lemon. Its name means Dutch, but the sauce is French, probably born in Normandy.

The children are where the five earn their keep. Melt grated Gruyère and Parmesan into a warm béchamel and it becomes Mornay, the golden cheese sauce that bubbles on top of a gratin. Stir a sharp reduction of tarragon, shallot and vinegar into hollandaise and you have béarnaise, the classic steak sauce, with the same egg-and-butter emulsion underneath.

The family tree is older than Escoffier: in 1833 the chef Antonin Carême ranked four great sauces, espagnole, velouté, béchamel and allemande, and seventy years later Escoffier demoted allemande to a child of velouté and raised tomato and hollandaise to mother rank, the two sauces that break the roux pattern.

Colour changes a roux's power in a surprising direction: the darker you cook it, the weaker it thickens, because long heat breaks down the starch that does the thickening. A chocolate-brown roux has only about a quarter of a white roux's thickening power, which is why the near-black roux of a Cajun gumbo is prized for its toasty flavour rather than its body.

The brown sauce's proudest child is demi-glace, French for half-glaze: equal parts espagnole and brown stock, reduced by half into a dark, glossy, syrupy base for sauces such as bordelaise.

the-flatbread-family-and-the-pita-pocket.context_blurb:
Flatbreads are probably the oldest breads in the world, and nearly every cuisine has one: Mexico's tortilla, Ethiopia's injera, India's naan and chapati, the Middle East's pita, Armenia's lavash. Each is a thin round of dough baked fast on a very hot surface, and each one's softness, shape and staying power comes from its own trick.

The pita is the one with a pocket: slit a warm pita along its edge and the two sides pull apart around a hollow pouch, ready to be stuffed with falafel and salad. That hollow is made by steam, not yeast: in an oven at around 450 to 475°F, the water inside the thin dough turns to steam faster than it can escape, the trapped steam balloons the round and forces its top and bottom crusts apart, and when the bread cools and sinks, the gap stays.

Naan goes for softness, and its secret is yogurt, worked into the dough along with some milk and ghee to make the bread pillowy and tender. The dough is then pressed against the inside of a tandoor, a clay oven that can reach 900°F.

Lavash, the flatbread of Armenia, is rolled just two or three millimetres thin, and the baker slaps it onto the scorching inner wall of a clay oven, the tonir, where it bakes through in under a minute. Village bakers dried whole stacks of it to last three to six months, and to turn a stiff, cracker-hard sheet back into a soft wrap, they simply sprinkled it with water.

Markook, the paper-thin bread of Lebanon and Syria, is baked on a saj, an iron griddle that bulges upward in a dome, like a bowl turned upside down. Heated from below by a wood fire, the dome lets the huge, almost see-through sheet of dough drape over its curve and cook in seconds. The tenth-century cookbook writer Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq already described such bread as large, paper-thin and unleavened.

the-forks-scandalous-slow-arrival.context_blurb:
Picture a fine European dinner table in 1500: pewter plates, cups, knives and spoons, and food eaten largely with the fingers. The table fork, which now seems as basic as a plate, spent some seven centuries creeping across Europe, mocked and scorned for much of the way.

The fork was the last of the three everyday eating tools to arrive: for most of history Europeans ate with their fingers, a knife and a spoon, and the personal fork became normal on most of the continent's tables only in the 1700s.

Its first known appearance in Europe was a scandal. Around 1004 a Byzantine princess, Maria Argyropoulina, came to Venice as the bride of the Doge's son, and at the feast she would not touch her food with her fingers: her servants cut every dish into small pieces, and she speared the morsels on a little two-pronged golden fork. A monk, Peter Damian, wrote about it in disgust, and to Venetians who ate with their hands the whole performance looked shockingly decadent.

Italy took to the fork centuries ahead of everyone else, and food historians credit pasta: long, slippery, sauce-coated strands are nearly impossible to manage with fingers or a spoon, but they gather neatly on a fork's prongs, so the fork spread wherever the pasta went.

North of the Alps the fork stayed a joke for more than a century, and English writers sneered at it as an unmanly Italian affectation, a vain, dainty way to eat. Queen Elizabeth I owned several forks, yet she went on eating with her fingers like nearly everyone at her table.

Once the fork took over the job of spearing food and lifting it to the mouth, the table knife no longer needed a sharp point. Tradition says Cardinal Richelieu had knife tips filed round in about 1637, disgusted by guests picking their teeth with them, and in 1669 Louis XIV banned pointed table knives altogether, which is why a dinner knife still has a blunt, rounded end.

the-four-bbq-regions.context_blurb:
Barbecue in America means meat cooked low and slow in wood smoke for hours, until tough cuts turn tender. Across the South it splits into fiercely defended regional styles, and the differences come down to three things: which animal goes on the smoker, what sauce goes on the meat, and how it reaches the table.

Most of the South smokes pork, but Texas, ranch country built on cattle rather than pig farms, made beef its barbecue, above all thick slices of smoked brisket.

Eastern North Carolina goes the other way. Pitmasters there roast the entire hog for a day over hardwood coals and chop the meat from every part of it together. Their old boast is that they use every bit of the pig except the squeal. The chopped pork gets no thick red sauce, only a thin, sharp dressing of vinegar and hot red pepper, because the vinegar's acid cuts through the fatty richness of the pork and keeps each bite from tasting heavy.

The thick, red, sticky-sweet sauce most people picture when they hear the words barbecue sauce belongs to Kansas City, and its dark sweetness comes from molasses stirred into a tomato base. Down the Mississippi in Memphis, the pride of the house is a rack of dry ribs: pork ribs crusted in spice rub, smoked, and served with no sauce mopped on at all, unlike wet ribs basted before, during and after cooking.

Kansas City also gave the world burnt ends, the dark, chewy, fatty cubes cut from the point of a smoked brisket, and they began as scraps that Arthur Bryant's smokehouse simply gave away for free. Then in 1972 the food writer Calvin Trillin called the burned edges of the brisket the best thing on the menu, and today fans pay extra for them.

The rarest sauce of all is the bright mustard-yellow Carolina Gold of South Carolina's Midlands, a legacy of German immigrants who travelled south from Pennsylvania along the Great Wagon Road in the 1700s and brought their homeland's habit of eating mustard with meat.

the-french-omelette.context_blurb:
The French omelette is a test of a cook's hands. It uses little more than eggs, butter, salt and pepper, takes about a minute, and leaves nowhere to hide: a perfect one is pale, creamy yellow all over, soft inside and neatly shaped. Young French cooks are judged on it, and the great chef Jacques Pépin has spent a career explaining it.

The first rule is no colour: a classic French omelette never browns, and a golden-brown one means the cook let the pan get too hot. Pépin explains that browning toughens the egg white's proteins, and he wants the omelette tender and soft.

The secret lies in the first seconds, when the cook keeps the eggs in constant motion, stirring and shaking as fast as he can so the curds stay as small as possible. Left alone, the eggs would set into one solid, rubbery sheet; kept moving, they become a soft, creamy mass.

On purpose, the cook leaves the centre soft and a little runny, a style the French call baveuse, from the verb baver, which means to drool or slobber. That soft, drooling heart shows skill; it is not a sign of undercooking.

Then comes the shape: Pépin rolls the omelette in the pan like a carpet and turns it out seam-side down as a slim, smooth oval, pointed at both ends. An American diner omelette is a different dish, not a worse one, cooked hotter into a big, sturdy curd that is browned and folded so it can carry cheese and ham.

The world's most famous omelette comes from Mont-Saint-Michel, the island abbey off Normandy that the Atlantic tide cuts off from the mainland. By 1873 Annette Poulard, known as Mère Poulard, was keeping an inn there with her husband. Travellers could turn up at any hour, cold and hungry, whenever the tide let them cross, so she needed a dish she could cook in minutes the moment they walked in, and her omelette, served at once while the rest of the meal was prepared, became famous across France.

the-french-precision-cuts-julienne-bruno.context_blurb:
Classical French kitchens give every knife cut a name and a size, so a chef can call out one word and get exactly the shape he wants. Pieces that match in size cook in the same time and look alike on the plate, which is why learning the cuts is one of the first jobs of a cooking student.

The most basic is the julienne, the matchstick cut: long, thin, square-sided sticks about an eighth of an inch across and one to two inches long, like the carrot strips scattered over a salad. Cut from a potato, the same matchstick is called an allumette, French for matchstick, the cut behind the thin fries called pommes allumettes, and a julienne sliced to half that thickness is a fine julienne.

Leaves need their own method, the chiffonade: the cook stacks basil or mint leaves, rolls the pile into a tight bundle and slices across it, and the roll falls open into fine green ribbons.

The tiny, even cubes called brunoise, which sparkle in clear soups, are not diced straight from the vegetable: the cook first cuts long thin sticks, a julienne, then gathers the bundle and chops straight across it, so each stick falls apart into little eighth-inch cubes.

The word julienne is older than the cut: in French cookbooks of the 1720s it named a clear vegetable soup, said to honour a cook called Jules or Julien, and the matchstick cut probably took its name from the vegetables sliced fine for that broth.

Hardest of all is the tourné, or turned cut: the cook rotates a piece of potato, carrot or turnip against a short, hooked paring knife known as a bird's beak and carves it by hand into a smooth, seven-sided barrel about two inches long, tapered at each end. It exists so that every piece cooks and plates exactly alike.

the-fruit-in-disguise-culinary-vegetable.context_blurb:
Ask a cook and a botanist whether a tomato is a fruit and you start an argument both of them can win. Cooks sort food by taste and use: savoury things served at dinner are vegetables, sweet things are fruit. Botanists sort by where a part grows on the plant, and their rule turns the vegetable aisle upside down.

To a botanist, a fruit is any part that grows from a fertilised flower and carries the seeds inside, because carrying the seeds is a fruit's whole job; sweet or savoury makes no difference. By that rule a tomato is a fruit, since it swells from the plant's flower with its seeds tucked inside, even though every kitchen treats it as a savoury vegetable.

The same rule catches many foods in the vegetable aisle: a bell pepper grew from a flower and carries its seeds inside, so botanically it is a fruit, and so are cucumber, eggplant, zucchini and green beans. Carrots, celery and lettuce, by contrast, come from roots, stems and leaves, so those really are vegetables. When a botanist and a chef argue over a cucumber, both are right, because the two words answer different questions. Fruit is the botanist's word for where a part grew; vegetable is the cook's word for how a food is eaten, savoury and with the main course, and it means nothing in botany.

Rhubarb is the trick in reverse: kitchens sweeten it and bake it into pies as a fruit, but the rosy part we eat is a leaf stalk, the long stalk that holds up the plant's big leaf, and it never grew from a flower or carried a seed. A peanut plays a name trick, because botanically it is not a nut at all but a legume, a pod like a pea's or a bean's, while each kernel of corn counts as a grain, a fruit holding a single seed. Even a pumpkin is a fruit, and a special kind: botanists call it a pepo, which is simply a berry with a hard, tough rind, and watermelons and cucumbers are pepos too.

Stone fruits such as cherries, peaches and plums wrap their flesh around one seed sealed in a hard, woody pit, and of the fruits that turn up on a pizza only the olive is built that way, a bitter, savoury stone fruit that proves fruit need not mean sweet. The avocado looks like a stone fruit but fails the test, because the layer around its big seed is soft and thin rather than a woody pit, so botanists file it with the berries, alongside the grape: a berry can hold one large seed or many small ones.

The argument once reached the Supreme Court of the United States. The importer John Nix, facing a tariff that taxed imported vegetables but let fruit in free, argued that his tomatoes were fruit. In 1893 Justice Horace Gray agreed that botanically they were, but ruled that in everyday speech, and so for the tax collector, the tomato is a vegetable, because it is served with dinner rather than as dessert.

A true berry, in strict botanical terms, is a fleshy fruit that develops from just one ovary of one flower and holds its seeds within, and the banana fits that rule perfectly, so a banana is a true berry; the tiny dark specks down its middle are its undeveloped seeds. The strawberry fails the same test: its red flesh is a swollen flower base, and each speck on its skin is really a tiny fruit in its own right, called an achene, with one true seed inside it. A strawberry wears its fruits on the outside.

the-great-swap-two-directions-across-the.context_blurb:
When Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, he set off the biggest swap of foods in history, which historians call the Columbian Exchange. Plants and animals that had lived on only one side of the ocean crossed to the other, in both directions, and within a few centuries they had changed what people ate, and how many people there were, on every continent.

Before 1492, corn, chocolate, potatoes and tomatoes grew only in the Americas, which is why medieval Italian cooking had no tomatoes, Irish stew had no potatoes and Swiss chocolate did not exist. Animals crossed too: the Spanish found the Aztecs raising the turkey, a plump bird native to the Americas, and shipped it home, so that within a lifetime European farmers kept it in their own barnyards.

The fiery heat of Indian and Thai cooking is newer than it tastes, because chili peppers are a New World plant: Portuguese traders carried them to India in the 1500s and rebuilt the cooking of a region that had never known heat like it. The tomato had a slower welcome, since for generations after it reached Europe many people believed the fruit was poisonous and grew the plant only for show. The fear was wrong, and the tomato later became the heart of Italian sauce.

The biggest change was in sheer numbers of people. In China, whose population boomed in the 1600s and 1700s, hungry farmers climbed into dry hill country where neither rice nor wheat would grow, and there the American sweet potato thrived, giving far more calories per acre; along with maize and white potatoes, it helped China's population roughly triple between 1500 and 1900. In Europe the hero was the potato, an Andean plant, not an Irish one, which grew so well in cool northern soil that the economists Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian credit it with about a quarter of the Old World's population growth from 1700 to 1900.

How the sweet potato reached China is a story in itself: in 1593 the Spanish rulers of the Philippines banned taking the plant out, and, as the tale is told, Chen Zhenlong, a merchant from Fujian, smuggled the vines aboard by wrapping them round a rope on his ship's rail. A drought struck Fujian the following year, the smuggled crop fed the hungry, and grateful locals later built a Temple of the First Sweet Potato.

The crops crossed to Africa as well: in the 1500s Portuguese traders brought cassava, a starchy root from Brazil that swells in dry, poor ground where grain crops fail, and over the centuries it pushed aside the old staples, sorghum and millet, to become one of Africa's great foods.

the-ice-trade-selling-new-england-winter.context_blurb:
In the 1800s, before electric refrigerators, a Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor built a fortune on an idea that sounded like a joke: sell New England's winter to the tropics. His ships carried pond ice to the Caribbean, the American South and even India, and for a century natural ice kept drinks cold and food fresh in places that had never seen frost.

A family's summer ice was harvested the winter before: crews sawed the frozen surface of New England ponds into a chessboard of two-foot blocks, once the ice was at least eighteen inches thick, and stacked them in ice houses to sell through the hot months. Henry David Thoreau watched men cut up his own Walden Pond this way.

Tudor's first voyage, in 1806, went to the Caribbean island of Martinique, and a Boston paper mocked the plan as a slippery speculation. The hard part was keeping the ice frozen at sea, and his answer was sawdust, a cheap waste product of New England's lumber mills, packed thick around blocks stacked tight like brickwork, which slowed the melting enough for a cargo to survive months at sea.

In a port where nobody had ever tasted ice, Tudor first had to create a craving, so he gave free ice to bartenders, betting that anyone who had his drinks cold for a week would never accept them warm again.

His boldest run, in 1833, carried ice some 16,000 miles to Calcutta in India, a city that had thought the whole idea a joke. After four months at sea, the brig Tuscany opened its hold and found that most of the cargo had survived as solid ice, about 100 of its 180 tons, because the sawdust had done its job. Calcutta became Tudor's most profitable route.

The trade lasted about a century and died out by the 1930s, beaten by machines that turned out ice in any town at any time of year, with no frozen pond or long voyage needed: factory ice overtook pond ice by 1914, and home electric refrigerators finished the job.

the-incredible-egg-yolk-white-and-what-e.context_blurb:
Crack an egg and it looks simple, but its two parts are different tools. The yolk holds nearly all the fat, colour and vitamins, plus a molecule that makes oil and water get along; the white is mostly protein and water, ready to set firm in heat or whip into a foam. Good cooks use each for its own job.

The yolk is a natural emulsifier: it carries lecithin, a molecule that coats droplets of oil and links them to water, so the oil and vinegar in mayonnaise stay blended in one smooth, creamy sauce instead of splitting into layers. The same trick holds together hollandaise and custard.

Boil an egg too long and a grey-green ring appears around the yolk, made when heat drives sulfur out of the white to meet iron in the yolk, forming iron sulfide. It is harmless, and plunging the eggs into cold water as soon as they finish cooking prevents it.

Very fresh eggs are the hardest to peel, because as an egg ages, carbon dioxide seeps out through its porous shell and the white grows more alkaline; that alkaline white grips the shell's inner membrane less, so an older egg's shell lifts away in clean sheets.

The white's great talent is foam, and foam is fragile. Even the smallest bit of fat, a speck of yolk or a greasy film on the bowl, stops whites from whipping up, because fat gets in the way of the proteins that cage the air. French pastry cooks have gone the other way since the 1700s, whipping whites in copper bowls: a trace of copper from the bowl binds to the egg proteins, making the foam steadier and hard to overbeat.

the-irish-potato-famine.context_blurb:
In the 1840s the poor of Ireland lived on the potato almost alone, and when a blight destroyed the crop several years running, roughly a million people died and another million fled the country. The Great Famine is a food story through and through: one crop, one variety, a microscopic invader, and food that kept leaving the island.

A grown labourer ate twelve to fourteen pounds of boiled potatoes over a day, and he washed them down with buttermilk, the sour liquid left after churning butter, too poor to sell and so kept for the family's own table. Ireland leaned on the potato even beyond its people: roughly one potato in every three was grown to feed livestock, not humans.

Most poor families grew one variety above all, the Lumper, a big, watery potato, not much prized for flavour, that gave heavy harvests even on the poor, wet land they farmed.

In 1845 the crop rotted in the fields, and the cause was a microscopic mould, a water mould now called Phytophthora infestans, carried from North America on ships, which turned the tubers into black, inedible slime. It ruined a third to half of the harvest that year and about three-quarters the next.

The failure was total because potatoes are grown from cuttings, pieces of the potato itself, not from seed, so every Lumper in Ireland was a near-identical clone, and a disease that could kill one could kill them all. With no variety to resist it, about one in eight Irish people died of hunger and disease within three years.

The poorest who fled crammed into cheap, crowded emigrant vessels so deadly that people called them coffin ships; of the more than 100,000 Irish who sailed for Canada in 1847, about one in five did not survive, and over 5,000 are buried at the quarantine island of Grosse Isle in Quebec.

The cruellest fact is that Ireland's farms kept producing grain, cattle and butter throughout, and much of it was shipped out of Ireland to Britain: in 1847 alone almost 4,000 ships carried food to Liverpool, Bristol, Glasgow and London while people starved at home. Historians still argue fiercely over how far the landlords and the government's free-market policy turned a crop failure into mass death.
