the-medieval-banquet-as-spectacle.context_blurb:
In a castle's great hall in the Middle Ages, a feast was theatre as much as dinner. Trumpets announced the dishes, cooks competed to astonish, and every detail, from where you sat to how a bird was carved, displayed the lord's wealth and each guest's rank. Much of the show was meant to be marvelled at more than eaten.

Rank began with the salt: the great salt cellar, a costly showpiece of pewter, silver or gold, stood at the host's right hand, and honoured guests sat above the salt near him while lesser folk sat below it, further down the table. In front of each diner there was no dish at all, only a trencher, a thick square or round cut from a loaf several days old, which held the meat and soaked up its sauce. Nor was there a fork: a diner brought his own belt-knife, used a spoon and his fingers, and English tables would not see forks in common use until the 1700s. The diners seldom ate the soggy trenchers; when the feast ended, the almoner usually collected them with the leftover broken meats and gave them out as charity to the poor waiting at the gates.

At Christmas the centrepiece was a roasted boar's head carried in on a gilded platter with rosemary and bay, an apple, or sometimes a lemon, set in its jaws; a carol first printed in 1521 still greets it.

The showiest dishes were birds. For a peacock, the cook skinned the bird with its plumage whole, roasted the body, then dressed it again in its own skin and feathers, gilding the beak and feet, so that it came to the table looking alive. Guests often applauded the gilded peacock rather than eating it, which was no great loss, since the meat beneath the feathers was famously tough, dry and tasteless. The Italian cook Martino da Como, in his cookbook of about 1465, even made the bird breathe fire: a little camphor wrapped in cotton wool, with some strong wine or spirit, went into the beak and was lit as the peacock was served.

Swan, the costliest bird of all, came crowned and garlanded, with a near-black sauce called chaudron, made from the swan's own blood and innards, spiced and sharpened with vinegar. The most monstrous dish was the cockentrice: cooks sewed the front half of a piglet to the back half of a capon, a young rooster, or the other way round, and roasted the creature whole.

Between courses came subtleties, edible sculptures that were often whole castles; at a banquet for Pope Clement VI in 1343, one castle had walls built of roasted birds and was peopled with re-dressed deer, boar, hares and goats.

Even carving was an art with rules, and a young nobleman served as carving esquire before his knighthood. A guide printed in 1508 gave every bird its own carving verb, so that a carver would lift a swan, disfigure a peacock and unbrace a mallard, and the wrong word or the wrong cut was a public disgrace.

the-medieval-spice-flex-and-the-rotten-m.context_blurb:
A popular story says medieval cooks drowned their meat in spices to hide the taste of rot. Food historians call that a myth: spices cost a fortune, and anyone who could buy them could easily buy fresh meat. In the medieval kitchen spices were a way to show off wealth, and some were nearly as good as money.

Black pepper was so precious that people counted out peppercorns to pay rents, taxes and dowries, which is why a tiny token payment that seals a deal in law is still called a peppercorn rent.

Rich medieval cooks also kept sugar in the locked spice chest, treating it as one more exotic spice, so a single meat dish might be seasoned with cinnamon, ginger, saffron and sugar together, long before cooks split sweet food from savoury.

Costliest of all was saffron, the dried red threads plucked from the heart of a purple crocus; each flower gives only three, so a single gram takes about 150 flowers picked by hand, and saffron has long been the most expensive spice in the world by weight.

the-mediterranean-pattern-and-the-detect.context_blurb:
The Mediterranean diet that doctors praise today was not invented in a laboratory. It was the daily fare of poor farming families in the villages of Greece and southern Italy in the 1950s, and an American scientist, Ancel Keys, made it famous while hunting for the cause of the heart attacks that were killing well-fed Americans.

The villagers' fat was olive oil, used for cooking in place of butter and poured over vegetables, bread and beans, and it is the signature of the whole pattern, which was low in red meat and sugar. The humblest part of their plates is the one modern fans forget: beans and other legumes, cheap, filling protein eaten almost every day alongside heaps of vegetables.

The puzzle that started Keys's work ran backwards to what anyone expected: the poor, plain-eating villagers had far less heart disease than rich Americans living on steak and butter, and Keys set out to find the reason. In his huge Seven Countries Study of thousands of middle-aged men, the very healthiest hearts belonged to the men of Crete, who lived on olive oil, wild greens, beans, bread and fruit, saving meat for the occasional feast.

At the opposite extreme, in North Karelia, in Finland's east, dairy farmers lived on butter and fatty meat and recorded one of the highest heart-attack death rates ever measured.

From those findings Keys and others drew a broader claim, that saturated fat itself causes heart disease, and it shaped fifty years of low-fat advice; today many researchers say the Mediterranean pattern still looks healthy but that the blanket verdict against saturated fat is disputed, since his study showed a link, not proof. The charge that Keys simply faked or cherry-picked his data is disputed too: the famous chart his critics attack came from a 1953 talk, before the Seven Countries Study began, and the study itself gathered fresh data on nearly 13,000 men.

the-mezze-table-a-spread-of-little-plate.context_blurb:
Across the eastern Mediterranean, in Lebanon, Syria, Turkey and Greece, a proper meal opens with mezze: a table crowded with little plates of dips, salads, pickles, cheeses and stuffed leaves, shared by everyone and picked at slowly with bread. Each small plate carries its own trick, and several carry a long history.

Real Levantine tabbouleh, a national dish of Lebanon, is not a wheat salad at all: it is mostly finely chopped parsley, eighty per cent parsley in one Palestinian chef's words, with only a little bulgur wheat for texture. Shop versions flip the balance and pile in the grain.

The smoky taste of baba ganoush comes from fire, not spice: the cook holds a whole eggplant over an open flame for about twenty minutes, until its skin is charred black and blistered and the flesh inside collapses into a soft, smoky pulp. Then the pulp is mashed with tahini, lemon, garlic and olive oil. The eggplant itself is a newcomer to the region: it came from South Asia, and it was Arab traders who spread it westward around the Mediterranean, so that it had arrived in Spain, then Muslim al-Andalus, by the 700s, while no ancient Greek or Roman writer had a name for it.

Labneh, the soft white cheese served with a pool of olive oil and a pinch of mint, needs no rennet and no ageing, because it is simply yogurt hung in a cloth bag until its watery whey drips away. Rolled into balls and sunk in olive oil, it keeps for more than a year without a fridge.

Dolma pack seasoned rice and herbs into small rolls wrapped in a grape leaf, which is simmered soft and eaten along with the filling; in Arabic the dish is called warak enab, which simply means grape leaves.

From Aleppo in northern Syria comes muhammara, a brick-red dip of fire-roasted red peppers whose rich body and gentle crunch come from ground walnuts. Its sweet-sour tang comes from pomegranate molasses, pomegranate juice boiled down until a whole pot shrinks to a dark, tart syrup, the tangy backbone of Levantine dressings and dips.

the-new-world-crossed-the-ocean-and-rema.context_blurb:
Much of what Africa eats today crossed the ocean in the last five centuries. Maize, cassava, chili peppers and tomatoes are all crops of the Americas that Portuguese ships carried to Africa after 1500, and the traffic ran both ways, for some of the world's favourite foods began in Africa.

Every chili pepper traces back to wild plants of the Americas, unknown in Africa and Asia before Columbus sailed in 1492; from the late 1490s Portuguese merchants carried chilies grown in Brazil to West and North Africa, where their heat quickly became a signature of local cooking.

Coffee travelled the other way, because wild coffee first grew in the cool highlands of Ethiopia, and the word itself is said to trace back to Ethiopia's Kaffa province. The famous legend of a goatherd whose goats danced after eating the red berries was not written down until 1671. Okra, too, is African, native to the north-east of the continent, and enslaved Africans carried both the plant and its Bantu name, ki ngombo, across the Atlantic, which is why Louisiana's okra stew is called gumbo.

Maize, now Africa's most important staple, eaten as ugali, nshima, sadza and pap, was bred about 9,000 years ago by farmers in southern Mexico from teosinte, a scrawny wild grass with no fat cob at all.

Cassava, the starchy Brazilian root behind fufu and garri, is poisonous raw, so West African cooks soak the roots in water for about three days and let them ferment before drying or cooking them.

Jollof rice, the red one-pot pride of Ghana and Nigeria, shows that a crop's arrival and a dish's birth are different dates: the tomato landed in Africa about five centuries ago, but the tomato-rich jollof cooked today is only about 200 years old, from the 1800s. Its name comes from the Wolof people of Senegal.

the-north-butter-south-oil-divide.context_blurb:
Italian cooking splits roughly in two over its fat. In the hot, dry south, olive oil goes into nearly every pan; in the cool north, close to the Alps, the cooking fat is something else. The split is a broad tendency rather than a hard border, but it shapes everything from pasta to cheese.

Northern Italy, the Alpine belt and Emilia-Romagna, is cattle country, so butter from its dairy herds goes into the pan, the sauce and the finished dish. The south's grip on olive oil grew stronger in the Middle Ages, when the Church's Lenten fasting rules banned butter and other animal fats for weeks at a time: olive oil broke no rule, and the south already had it on hand.

The pasta divides too: the north is the home of fresh pasta made with egg, golden tagliatelle and filled tortellini from Bologna and Emilia-Romagna, while the south's dried pasta is only durum wheat semolina and water, with no egg at all. The south could make dried pasta that kept for months because its hot, dry winds, above all in Sicily, air-dried the strands, while the cooler, damper north could not dry pasta well and ate its fresh pasta the same day.

In the mountain villages of Piemonte and Veneto, the daily food of poor families for generations was polenta, a thick yellow porridge of ground corn stirred for hours over the fire.

The north's surplus of cow's milk became two famous hard cheeses, Grana Padano and Parmigiano-Reggiano, made by ageing the big wheels for years until they turn hard enough to grate; the name Padano points to the Po Valley, where the dairy herds graze.

the-onion-family-bulbs-and-tears-alliums.context_blurb:
Onions, garlic, shallots, leeks, chives and scallions all belong to one plant family, the alliums. They share an underground way of life and a weapon: a set of sulfur compounds that gives them their bite, makes cooks cry, and melts into sweetness under slow heat.

An onion is a bulb, a short, squat stem buried underground and wrapped in fleshy leaves, and each ring you see in a sliced onion is one of those swollen storage leaves seen end-on, so the onion is a stack of fat leaf-bases, not a solid root. Even the crackly brown skin is made of leaves: it is the outermost layers, the same as the juicy rings inside, which dried out and turned brittle as the bulb aged, forming a papery wrapper.

Chop a raw onion and you tear open thousands of cells, mixing an enzyme with the onion's stored sulfur compounds; together they release a tiny, invisible cloud of sulfur gas that rises into your eyes and stings them, and your eyes make tears to wash it away. That chemistry was never aimed at you: wild onions and garlic evolved it to poison and drive off the insects, slugs, worms and fungi that would gnaw on the buried bulb, and your tears are a side effect of a weapon meant for pests.

A head of garlic splits into cloves, and each clove is a complete little storage bud in its own papery wrapper, so a gardener who plants just one clove grows an entire new garlic plant; garlic mostly copies itself this way instead of making seed. A whole clove barely smells, because its famous punch does not exist until the clove is crushed: breaking the cells lets an enzyme turn an odourless compound, alliin, into pungent allicin, so the smell is made on the spot by the damage.

Heat tames the whole family. Cooking breaks down the sharp allicin and destroys the enzyme that makes it, so a raw clove burns the tongue, but a head of garlic roasted slowly turns mild, sweet, brown and soft enough to spread.

the-overland-spice-road-and-why-europe-w.context_blurb:
For most of the Middle Ages, Europe's pepper, cinnamon and cloves came from the far side of the world, from India, Sri Lanka and the islands beyond, and passed through hand after hand on the way. Every pair of hands took its cut, and by the time the spices reached a European kitchen they were worth a fortune. Escaping those middlemen became one of the great goals of European kings.

Before any ship sailed round Africa, much of the spice moved overland in great camel caravans that crossed the deserts of Asia, hauling sacks of pepper, cinnamon and cloves thousands of miles toward the Mediterranean. From roughly the 700s to the 1400s, Venice and Italy's other sea republics held a near-monopoly on Europe's trade with the East, and by the late Middle Ages the great gateway was Venice, which landed more Eastern spice on its docks than any rival.

The prices were staggering. Pepper bought cheaply on India's Malabar Coast cost many times as much once Arab merchants had carried it west to the Mediterranean, and more again once Venetian merchants had shipped it on to Venice, so that relay of Arab and Venetian traders held most of the spice fortune.

When the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople in 1453, Europe feared pepper would vanish from its kitchens, yet pepper stayed about the same price for almost half a century, because Venice kept buying through a treaty with the Mamluk rulers of Egypt at Alexandria. The real break came in 1498, when Vasco da Gama reached India by sea and brought pepper home the direct way, halving Venice's prices and ending its monopoly.

the-passion-fruit-and-the-passion-of-chr.context_blurb:
The passion flower and its fruit sound as if they were named for romance, but the name is far older and darker. When missionaries from Spain and Portugal first saw the vine in the South American forests during the 1500s and 1600s, they found in its strange, intricate flower a picture of the most solemn story of their faith.

For them the Passion meant the Crucifixion of Jesus, his suffering and death on the cross: the word comes from the Latin passio, suffering, and has nothing to do with romantic love. They read the story into the flower part by part, and the frilly ring at its heart, the corona, a fringe that in some species holds 70 to 100 or more coloured threads, stood for the crown of thorns pressed onto Christ's head.

The same vine, native to southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina, gives the passion fruit, which Brazilians call maracujá, from the Tupi word murukuia. Cut one open and there is no solid flesh at all, only some 250 seeds, each wrapped in a little sac of tart, musky pulp, which goes into juice and into a fluffy mousse that is a classic Brazilian dessert.

the-peanut-that-buries-itself-a-legume-n.context_blurb:
The peanut is one of the great impostors of the kitchen. It is not a nut, it did not come from where most Americans think, and it grows in a way almost no other crop does: its pods ripen underground. It also helped rescue the worn-out farmland of the American South.

Botanists file the peanut with beans, peas and lentils in the legume family: its seeds grow inside a pod, just like peas in a pea pod, which breaks every rule for a true nut. The plant's wild home is South America, on the eastern side of the Andes, around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina and Brazil; Spanish and Portuguese traders carried it to Africa, and it reached North America aboard slave ships, which is why the Southern word goober comes from nguba, the Kongo name for it.

The peanut's little yellow flower lasts only about a day, and it fertilises itself, with no need for pollen from another flower or a visit from an insect. Then something strange happens: a stalk called a peg grows down from the base of the fertilised flower and drives the young pod into the soil, where the peanuts ripen in the dark, safe from animals and weather. Botanists call this rare habit geocarpy, fruit in the earth.

Like other legumes, the peanut carries bacteria in little nodules on its roots that pull nitrogen out of the air and fix it into the soil, refilling land that cotton and corn have drained, so a field that grew peanuts one year can grow a strong crop of corn the next.

At Tuskegee, the scientist George Washington Carver, who had been born into slavery, told the South's farmers to sow peanuts on fields that cotton had exhausted. When they ended up with more peanuts than anyone would buy, he answered by inventing some 300 new uses for them, from milk and flour to dyes, glue and shaving cream. In 1921 he showed product after product to a committee of Congress whose members had come to mock him and ended up giving him more time. One thing he did not invent was peanut butter: a Canadian pharmacist patented a peanut paste in 1884, and peanut pastes go back to the Aztecs.

the-pie-from-meat-coffin-to-apple-pie.context_blurb:
Pie began as a cooking pot you could carry. Medieval cooks sealed meat inside a thick case of pastry to bake it, keep it and move it, and only over centuries did the crust turn tender and buttery and the filling turn to sweet fruit, until the apple pie became a symbol of America.

Medieval English bakers called that stiff case a coffin, from coffyn, a word that meant a basket or box and had nothing to do with burial; it was a savoury shell of rye flour and water, baked several inches thick around the meat. The coffin also preserved the pie: sealed tight, the crust kept air away from the meat and its juices, so a pie kept far longer than bare meat and could travel in a saddlebag, and bakers sometimes poured melted fat through a hole in the lid to shut out the last of the air.

The English pork pie still stands up on its own walls because its pastry is a hot-water crust, made by melting fat in boiling water and beating in flour, which gives a warm, pliable paste that a baker can raise by hand into free-standing walls that bake firm enough to hold a heavy, juicy filling.

A flaky crust works the opposite way: the butter must stay cold and in solid flakes, so that in the hot oven the flakes melt and the water trapped inside them flashes into steam, prying the thin sheets of dough apart into crisp layers. To pre-bake an empty crust without it puffing or slumping, a cook lines it with paper and weighs it down with dried beans, tipped out before the filling goes in; the trick is called blind baking.

As American as apple pie is a strange saying, since the apple is an Old World fruit and the oldest known apple pie recipe is English, from about 1381, baked in a coffin crust. The classic pie whose filling truly is native to the Americas is pumpkin pie, made from a squash that Indigenous farmers grew for thousands of years.

the-poison-ivy-family-at-your-dinner-tab.context_blurb:
Mangoes, pistachios, cashews and the tangy spice sumac sound like a random shopping list, but botanists put them all in one plant family, Anacardiaceae, the cashew family. Its most notorious member is a wild plant that hikers dread, poison ivy, and several of the foods share its irritating chemistry.

Mango and poison ivy are close relatives: the fruit's skin, sap and leaves carry urushiol, the same rash-causing oil, so eating a mango with its skin on can leave some people with an itchy rash on the lips, a mild poison-ivy reaction that peeling the fruit prevents.

The cashew is worse, because its raw shell is coated with a caustic oil, chemically related to poison ivy's, that blisters and burns bare skin, so cashews reach the shops already shelled, not in the shell for you to crack at home. Even the bags labelled raw have been treated: every commercial cashew is roasted at high heat, or steamed, to destroy that oil, which also leaves the tough shell brittle enough to crack.

Nothing is wasted. Factories squeeze tons of that oil from the empty shells, and its tough resin goes into brake linings for cars, along with varnishes and paints, so the same seed gives us a snack and a car part.

Sumac, the sour, lemony red spice of Middle Eastern cooking and za'atar, comes from a shrub of the same family, and it has a toxic relative, poison sumac; the safe way to tell them apart in the wild is the berries, red clusters on the edible shrub and white on the poisonous one.

the-potato-a-stem-that-grew-underground-.context_blurb:
The potato looks like the plainest food on the table, yet nearly everything about it surprises a botanist. It is not a root, it comes from the high Andes, it is planted without seed, and it went from feared foreigner to the food that fed Europe's cities, and, in Ireland, to the heart of a catastrophe.

A potato is a swollen stem, not a root: it forms at the tip of a thin underground stem, called a stolon, which the plant stuffs with starch through the summer, so botanists call it a stem tuber. Its eyes prove it, because each eye is a bud, just like the buds spaced along a stem above ground, a sleeping growth point that can wake and push out a shoot. That is also how farmers grow it: instead of seed, they plant chunks of last year's potatoes, each with at least one eye, and every new plant that grows is a clone of its parent.

The potato began in the Andes, in South America, where farmers near Lake Titicaca, between Peru and Bolivia, domesticated it some 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, thousands of years before it reached Europe. The Andean highlands still grow more than 4,000 native kinds, and their most striking feature is colour: reds, purples and blues, as well as golds.

Andean farmers also invented a freeze-dried potato, chuño: on the high plateau they left potatoes out to freeze solid in the bitter night, then trod on them with their bare feet under the strong daytime sun to press the water out, and the result lasts for decades; it once fed Inca soldiers on the march.

The sweet potato is only a distant relative: it is the swollen root of a vine in the morning glory family, while the true potato is a stem from the nightshade family. The potato's own nightshade kinship shows in its rarely seen fruit, small green berries that look like tiny green tomatoes, each full of seeds and too toxic to eat.

A green potato is a warning, but the green itself is harmless chlorophyll, made when the tuber sits in light. The danger is that the same light also tells the potato to build up solanine, a natural toxin, most of which sits in and just under the skin, so peeling or cutting away the green removes most of it.

Europe's first potato eaters were few, and many people refused to touch it: it ripened out of sight underground, it was kin to the deadly nightshades, and the Bible never mentioned it, so wary Europeans called it the devil's apples and shunned it as unclean. Rulers had to push. In 1756 Frederick the Great of Prussia ordered his peasants to plant potatoes against famine, earning the nickname the potato king, and admirers still leave potatoes on his grave.

Farmers finally took it up for a blunt reason: an acre of potatoes grows far more food than an acre of grain, more calories per field than even maize or rice, and economists credit it with much of the population growth and city-building in Europe and Asia between 1700 and 1900.

The same clone trick brought disaster to Ireland, where the poor lived on a single variety, the Lumper: when blight struck in 1845, every plant was an identical copy with the same lack of defence, so the whole crop rotted at once, and about a million people died.

the-potato-remade-the-old-world.context_blurb:
Farmers in the Andes of South America grew the potato for thousands of years before Spanish ships carried it to Europe in the 1500s. For two centuries many Europeans scorned it; then, within a single lifetime, it spread across the continent's fields and fed a boom in people and cities that reshaped the Old World.

In the Andean highlands of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador, farmers still grow more than 4,000 native kinds, bred over centuries to survive at 11,000 to 14,000 feet, and visitors are astonished by their colours, bright reds, purples and blues. Chuño, a dried potato that lasts for years, is made by families who spread the tubers on flat ground and stomp on the piles barefoot, almost dancing, to crush out the water and rub off the skins, repeating the work for more than a week.

Europeans had a reason to be wary: the potato belongs to the nightshade family, which includes the poisonous deadly nightshade, though the same family holds two ordinary dinner vegetables, the tomato and eggplant, and the tuber itself is a safe everyday food. France was the stubbornest foe, sneering at potatoes as pig food and wrongly blaming them for spreading leprosy; a well-known tale, doubted by historians, says it banned the crop outright in 1748, and not until 1772 did the Paris Faculty of Medicine declare potatoes fit to eat.

Even then the French held back, so, as the famous story goes, Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, a pharmacist with the French army, sowed potatoes on land the king, Louis XVI, had given him and set armed guards over the field by day. Then he took the guards away at night, so curious villagers crept in, stole the valuable-looking crop and planted it in their own gardens. Parmentier had lived on potatoes as a prisoner of war in Prussia, and France still honours him in hachis Parmentier, its cottage pie.

After 1750, farmers from Ireland to Poland ploughed up grain to plant potatoes, for one blunt reason: a field of potatoes feeds far more people than the same field of wheat or rye, yielding about three times the food energy of wheat. Two economists, Nancy Qian and Nathan Nunn, worked out that the potato drove about a quarter of all the growth in the Old World's population, and in its cities, between 1700 and 1900.

the-roman-convivium.context_blurb:
A grand Roman dinner, the convivium, was a long evening of food, wine and talk in the house of a wealthy host, and it looked very little like a modern meal. Guests lay on couches, ate with their fingers and worked through course after course, while the richest hosts tried to dazzle them with luxuries and tricks.

Romans ate their banquets lying down, each guest stretched on his side along a couch beside a low table, a leisurely posture that marked the civilised life while slaves carried in the courses. The dining room took its name from those couches: the triclinium, meaning three couches, set in a U shape around the table, three diners to a couch, with the open fourth side left clear for serving. Every diner propped himself on his left elbow, because most people were right-handed, and lying on the left side left the stronger right hand free to reach for food.

The story of Romans running off to a vomitorium to empty their stomachs and eat more is a myth: a vomitorium was a passageway in an amphitheatre that let a packed crowd pour out, from the Latin vomere, to spew forth, and the Colosseum had 80 of them.

The favourite sauce on every table, for rich and poor alike, was garum, made from fish and salt left to cure in the sun until the fish broke down into a pungent, deeply savoury liquid, the ketchup of the empire. A formal dinner ran in three acts, from an opening course of eggs and salty tidbits through the main tables of roasts and stews to a sweet closing course of fruit and honey, which is why the poet Horace could sum up a whole dinner as from egg to apples.

Rome borrowed reclining from the Greek symposium, where only men lay on the couches, but changed one rule that shocked Greeks: respectable Roman wives and daughters reclined openly beside the men.

The richest hosts competed to astonish. In Petronius's comic novel the Satyricon, the vulgar millionaire Trimalchio pretends his cook forgot to gut a roast pig, and when the belly is slit, cooked sausages and blood puddings tumble out like its own insides. The same feast serves dormice coated in honey and dusted with poppy seeds, a luxury so decadent that a Roman censor once banned dormice from the table. Farmers fattened the little rodents in the dark inside a glirarium, a pierced earthenware pot ribbed with ramps and stocked with acorns and chestnuts, named from glis, the Latin for dormouse.

the-salt-wars.context_blurb:
Salt is the one rock people eat, and for most of history it was a treasure. Today it is better known as a health worry: doctors warn that a salty diet pushes blood pressure up, while a smaller group of researchers argues that the warnings go too far. Both sides agree on one thing, that the body cannot live without it.

Sodium carries the electrical signals of the body: each time a nerve fires, sodium rushes into the cell to make the signal, and the same kind of signal tells a muscle to contract, so without it you could not think a thought or move a finger. Table salt is sodium and chloride bonded into crystals, about 40 per cent sodium by weight, and only the sodium half matters to the health debate, which is why food labels list sodium rather than salt.

In the medieval Sahel, south of the Sahara, salt was so scarce, and gold so plentiful, that traditional accounts tell of camel caravans hauling salt across the desert to be traded weight for weight against gold.

The case for cutting back rests on simple physics: sodium draws water with it, so extra sodium in the blood pulls water into the bloodstream, raising the volume of blood and with it the pressure, which hurts salt-sensitive people most. The American Heart Association urges most Americans to eat less.

Critics point to the PURE study, which followed more than 80,000 people in 18 countries: heart risk rose clearly only where communities averaged more than 5 grams of sodium a day, and in the communities eating the least the risk crept back up again, a J-shaped curve that its lead author, Andrew Mente, read as a healthy middle range. The finding is contested, and defenders of low-salt advice argue that people who are already sick may simply eat less, so the debate remains open.

Whichever side is right, the salt shaker is a small part of the story: health agencies estimate that about 70 per cent of the sodium Americans eat is already inside packaged and restaurant foods, such as cold cuts, cheese, bread and canned soup, many of which do not even taste salty.

the-sandwich-and-the-earl.context_blurb:
The sandwich carries the name of an English nobleman, and around that name grew one of the best-known stories in food history: a gambler who would not leave his game of cards. Historians now doubt the story, and the idea of meat between bread is far older than the earl.

The food is named after an English nobleman, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, John Montagu, who lived from 1718 to 1792; it took his title rather than his family name, or we might be eating a montagu for lunch. The title came first from a place: when the earldom was created in 1660 for the naval commander Edward Montagu, he named it after Sandwich, an old port town in Kent, as a compliment to the town his fleet lay off before it sailed to bring Charles II home.

As the legend goes, the fourth earl was so lost in a card game around 1762 that he would not stop to eat, and asked for cold meat between two slices of bread so he could eat with one hand and keep grease off the cards; other players began asking for the same as Sandwich. The tale comes from a gossipy French travel writer who never even named the earl.

Rodger, the earl's biographer, points out that Montagu ran Britain's navy three separate times, as head of the Admiralty, and was buried in work, so the first sandwich was more likely a quick meal eaten at his crowded desk than over a game of cards.

Meat in bread is far older still: around 1,800 years before the earl, the Jewish sage Hillel the Elder wrapped Passover lamb and bitter herbs in matzah, and Jews still eat that bite at the Seder, calling it the Hillel sandwich.

the-saturated-fat-reversal.context_blurb:
For half a century, official advice told Americans to fear saturated fat, the fat in butter, cheese and red meat. In recent decades big studies have led many researchers to soften that warning, while others defend it, which makes saturated fat one of the most argued-over questions in nutrition. Some parts of the story are firm; others are still open.

A rough rule sorts the fats: those that stay solid at room temperature, like butter, lard and cheese, are mostly saturated fat, while oils that pour, like olive and corn oil, are mostly unsaturated. Coconut oil breaks the pattern: it comes from a plant, yet more than four-fifths of its fat is saturated, more than butter or lard, so it sets solid and waxy in a cool kitchen. Among the animal fats, butter is the most saturated, about two-thirds of its fat, while pork lard and beef tallow are only about two-fifths saturated.

The fear traces to the American researcher Ancel Keys, who argued that saturated fat raised blood cholesterol and so caused heart disease, and who in 1958 launched the Seven Countries Study, following thousands of middle-aged men from the United States to Japan; its data became the foundation of decades of low-fat advice. One part of that old view still holds: a diet heavy in saturated fat dependably raises LDL cholesterol, the kind a doctor measures at a checkup and calls bad.

Later research added nuance, because saturated fat also raises the good HDL cholesterol, and it tends to push LDL toward large, fluffy particles rather than the small, dense ones more strongly linked to heart risk.

The cruel twist of the anti-butter decades is that many families traded butter for margarine and shortening, made by pumping hydrogen through vegetable oil, a process that filled them with trans fat, the fat that later research tied clearly to heart disease.

In 2010 a team led by Patty Siri-Tarino combined 21 studies covering almost 348,000 people and reported that those who ate more saturated fat showed no clear rise in heart disease or stroke, a turning point for critics of the old advice. Defenders answered: the American Heart Association replied in 2017 with trials in which replacing butter and lard with polyunsaturated vegetable oil lowered heart disease by roughly 30 per cent, which it likened to the effect of a statin. The argument goes on.

the-screaming-hot-pan-and-the-dancing-dr.context_blurb:
Put a pan on the stove, wait, and flick on a few drops of water, and the drops will tell you whether it is ready. When the metal is hot enough, the water does something strange: instead of boiling away, it rolls into beads that skate over the surface. Physicists call this the Leidenfrost effect, and it is a cook's best free thermometer.

The first rule of browning is to get the empty pan really hot before the food goes in: a steak laid in a cool pan stews in the liquid it leaks, turns a dull grey and sticks, while a properly heated surface sears the outside the moment it lands.

The water test shows when you are there: in a pan that is not ready, drops hiss and vanish, but in a hot enough pan they gather into round beads that skate and skitter all over the metal. Each bead rides on a thin cushion of its own steam, which holds it off the metal and slows its boiling.

The pan must be far hotter than boiling for this to happen: water boils at 212°F, but the dance only starts at about 380 to 400°F, roughly twice the boiling point.

The same steam cushion explains a famous MythBusters stunt, done with expert safety precautions: the hosts dipped wet fingers into lead melted at about 850°F and pulled them out unhurt, because the water on their skin flashed into steam and, for a split second, held the metal away. It is a real burn and poisoning hazard that nobody should ever try.

the-sear-and-the-brown-crust-maillard-vs.context_blurb:
The brown crust on a seared steak, the gold of toast and the amber of caramel all look like the same thing, food cooked darker. They are really two different chemical reactions, often running side by side: the Maillard reaction, which needs sugar and protein, and caramelization, which needs sugar alone. Both make flavours the raw food never had.

In the Maillard reaction, named for the French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912, the food's sugars react with its own protein, through its amino acids, and build hundreds of new savoury flavours; it browns a seared steak and a bread crust, and it runs fast at around 280 to 330°F.

Caramelization is the other browning: heat plain sugar on its own and the sugar molecules themselves break apart into new compounds, with no protein involved, giving the amber, bittersweet, nutty taste of caramel and the crackly top of crème brûlée. It needs more heat than its partner, starting around 338°F for table sugar, which is why a pan of plain sugar has to get very hot before it turns.

So-called caramelized onions are really browned by both at once: some of their sugar caramelizes, but much of the toasty depth comes from the Maillard reaction, the onion's sugars meeting its own proteins. Even a cook's word for a dish can hide the second reaction at work in the pan.

the-serrated-knife-teeth-that-saw-bread-.context_blurb:
A smooth, straight kitchen knife is a fine tool for an onion, but it struggles with two foods: a crusty loaf and a ripe tomato. Both have a tough outside over a soft inside, and for both cooks reach for a serrated knife, a blade with a row of teeth along its edge that saws instead of pressing.

Push a smooth blade down on a crusty loaf and the soft crumb inside crushes flat before the edge can break through the hard crust, which is why bread knives have teeth that saw through the crust without squashing what lies beneath. A tomato has the same problem in another form: a dull straight edge skids off the tight, slippery skin and then bursts the flesh, but the pointed teeth of a serrated knife grip the skin at a few tiny high-pressure points and pierce it almost at once, with hardly any downward push.

A serrated knife works by sawing, not by one clean slice: each back-and-forth stroke opens a row of tiny splits in the surface, and those small cuts add up along the line of the blade until the slice comes free. The points only start the cut; the real slicing is done by the curved, scalloped hollows between the teeth, called gullets, which also cut down friction so the blade does not drag.

A serrated knife stays sharp for years because only the tips of its teeth touch the cutting board, so the gullets, the part that cuts, rarely rub against anything hard. The catch is that it cannot be sharpened flat on a stone; each gullet must be honed one at a time with a tapered rod.

the-sichuan-buzz-a-molecule-that-vibrate.context_blurb:
In the cooking of Sichuan, in south-west China, one spice produces a feeling found almost nowhere else in food. The Sichuan peppercorn, no relation to black pepper but the dried outer shell of a little lemony fruit that grows on the prickly ash, does not burn or cool the mouth. It makes the lips buzz, and scientists have worked out how.

Chew one for the first time and within seconds your lips start to tingle and fizz and then go half numb, a feeling Sichuan cooks call ma, which literally means numbing, and prize because it is nothing like a chili's burn. In the famous mala flavour of a Sichuan hot-pot, both feelings are built into the word: ma, the peppercorn's numbing buzz, and la, the chili's heat.

The two feelings travel on separate wires. A chili's capsaicin fools the nerves that sense heat, but the peppercorn's molecule, sanshool, works on the nerves of touch and vibration, which is why one bite can feel fiery and buzzing at the same instant.

In 2013 scientists in London asked volunteers to match the tingle against a small vibrating probe, and their answers landed at about fifty buzzes a second, right in the range the lip's light-touch nerves feel best.

Five years earlier, in 2008, a team in California had found how sanshool fakes that feeling: it jams the channels that normally act as an off-switch, keeping touch nerves quiet, so the nerves fire as if something were vibrating against the lips when nothing is touching them at all.

the-souffle.context_blurb:
A soufflé climbs tall and trembling above its dish without a grain of yeast or a pinch of baking powder. Everything that lifts it is air, beaten in by the cook, which makes it the most dramatic dish in the French kitchen, and the most fragile, because what rises must fall.

The engine is the egg whites, whisked into a stiff, glossy foam full of thousands of tiny air pockets, and the cook folds them into the flavoured base with a gentle lifting motion, never stirring, because stirring would burst the bubbles. The name says what happens next: soufflé comes from the French verb souffler, to blow, breathe or puff up, so the dish is simply the puffed-up one.

A savoury cheese soufflé builds its flavour on a thick béchamel, milk thickened with a butter-and-flour roux, while a sweet one uses pastry cream or fruit purée; either way, the base carries the flavour and the whites carry the lift.

In the hot oven two things happen at once: the trapped air swells as it warms, and the moisture in the batter turns to steam, and together they lift the soufflé high above the edge of the dish. French cooks warn against opening the oven door for roughly the first 25 minutes, because a rush of cold air can chill the soufflé and make it fall before its egg-white walls have set.

Even a perfect soufflé sinks within five or ten minutes of leaving the oven, because the air inside cools and shrinks and the tall structure settles, which is ordinary physics rather than a failed bake, and why the rule is to serve it the moment it comes out.

the-steel-in-the-blade-wootz-damascus-an.context_blurb:
Every kitchen knife is a bargain between two qualities. Hard steel takes a keen edge and keeps it, but it is brittle; softer steel bends instead of breaking, but dulls sooner. Medieval smiths chased both at once, and their most famous answer, the swirled Damascus blade, became a legend and then a lost art.

The surface of a true Damascus sword ripples with bands of light and dark, like moving water, and the swirls are no paint or engraving: they are the metal's own internal structure, forged into the steel and revealed by polishing and etching. Legends grew around its sharpness; in one tale a warrior held a Damascus sword edge-up and let a wisp of silk float down onto it, and the blade cut the silk clean in two. The tales are exaggerated, but such blades really did take and hold an unusually keen edge.

The swords were forged in Damascus, but the steel came from India: smiths in the south of India made this high-carbon crucible steel, called wootz, more than two thousand years ago, and shipped it west as cakes and ingots for over a thousand years.

Then the ripple stopped appearing, and Damascus steel became a lost art, until two metallurgists, Alfred Pendray and John Verhoeven, showed in 1998 that the pattern depended on tiny traces of elements such as vanadium carried in particular Indian ores; when those ores ran out, the swirl went with them.

Modern knives face the same bargain: a hard Japanese blade can be honed to a frightening sharpness that lasts for weeks, but harder steel is more brittle, so it can chip on bone or frozen food, while a softer German knife dulls sooner but survives the abuse.

Owners of carbon-steel knives welcome the mottled grey-blue film that slowly darkens the blade, because that patina is a stable, smooth layer that shields the steel and slows rust, unlike the orange, flaky rust that eats into the metal; a carbon knife is still wiped dry after every use.

the-sunday-roast-and-yorkshire-pudding.context_blurb:
For generations, Sunday in Britain has meant the Sunday roast: a big joint of meat roasting in the oven after church, potatoes crisping around it, gravy on the stove and, beside the meat, a puffy golden batter pudding named after Yorkshire. Each part of the meal has a thrifty story behind it.

The classic centrepiece is a roast joint of beef, a custom said to reach back to medieval England, when a squire rewarded his serfs on Sundays with whole oxen roasted on a spit. As the beef roasted, its hot fat and juices dripped into a pan beneath it, and thrifty northern cooks saved this fat, which they called dripping, to spread on bread through the week.

The Yorkshire pudding is not sweet at all: it is a savoury batter of just three plain ingredients, milk, eggs and plain flour, classically in equal measure, poured into smoking-hot fat. It was first called dripping pudding, because it was baked in that pan beneath the joint. It needs no yeast or baking powder, because in the fierce heat the water in the batter turns to steam, and the stretchy egg-and-gluten batter traps the steam and balloons into a hollow, crisp-edged dome; open the oven too early and the steam escapes and the rise collapses.

Pour the same batter over sizzling sausages and bake it, and you have toad in the hole, the oddest-named dish in the British kitchen, with no toads involved.

In ordinary homes a couple of centuries ago, the pudding was served first, as a course of its own drowned in gravy, before the meat: diners filled up on cheap batter so that a small, costly joint could stretch to feed everyone, and in poor homes the pudding was almost the whole meal.

the-tagine-a-pot-that-cooks-with-its-own.context_blurb:
In Morocco and across North Africa, the word tagine means a slow-cooked stew fragrant with spice, and it also means the pot. The pot is a shallow earthenware dish under a tall cone-shaped lid, and its odd shape is the secret of how the stew cooks.

The dish is named after its vessel: tagine, also spelled tajine, is both the stew and the cone-lidded clay pot it simmers in, so a family eating a tagine is eating out of a tagine.

The tall lid is a little rain machine: steam rises off the food, cools against the cone, condenses into droplets and runs back down onto the meat, so a whole stew needs only a splash of water and no stirring. A traditional tagine of bare, unglazed clay also takes part in the cooking, because the porous clay breathes and drinks up some of the cooking liquid; the American cookbook writer Paula Wolfert calls the result magical, a single pot that braises, steams and bakes at once.

A Moroccan lamb tagine mixes sweet and savoury in a way few European stews do: dried apricots and prunes simmer alongside the meat, along with ginger, cumin, cinnamon and saffron, and melt into the sauce over hours of slow cooking.

The sharp, salty citrus note comes from preserved lemons, cured whole in salt and their own juice until the peel softens, and Moroccan cooks almost always pair them with green olives.

the-tandoor-naan-and-tandoori-from-a-scr.context_blurb:
In northern India and Central Asia, cooks bake bread and roast meat in a tandoor, a tall, barrel-shaped oven with a charcoal or wood fire burning in its base. It runs far hotter than any home oven, and nearly everything about tandoori food, from blistered naan to red, smoky chicken, comes from that fierce heat.

A tandoor is built of thick clay, shaped like a giant vase, and that heavy clay, unlike the metal box of a kitchen oven, soaks up the fire's heat and radiates it back to blister bread and char meat. A working tandoor reaches about 480°C, roughly twice the top setting of a home oven, so a skewer of chicken lowered inside cooks through in just a few minutes.

The smoky taste is real fire cooking: as the chicken roasts on its skewer, its own melting fat and juices drip onto the glowing coals below and flare into smoke that rises back over the meat, something a sealed home oven cannot copy.

Naan is baked on the upright inner wall of the oven: the baker uses a cloth cushion called a gaddi to press the flattened dough against the hot clay, where it puffs and blisters in about a minute before being pried off with a hooked metal skewer.

Tandoori chicken starts a day early, in a marinade of thick yogurt and spices, whose mild acid and enzymes gently tenderize the surface of the meat by breaking down its proteins, while its milk sugars help form the crisp crust in the fire. The famous red-orange colour comes from ground spices in that marinade, above all Kashmiri red chilli, prized because it gives a deep red with very little heat, along with cayenne and turmeric; some restaurants once cheated with food dye, but the home version never needed it.

The Delhi chef Kundan Lal Gujral is also credited with first roasting chicken in a tandoor. As the story goes, he hated to waste the cooked pieces left unsold each night in the days before fridges, so he simmered them in a rich gravy of tomato and butter, and that became butter chicken, born at his Moti Mahal restaurant in the late 1940s.

the-three-sisters.context_blurb:
Centuries before any European ship landed, the farming peoples of eastern North America planted three crops side by side in small hills of earth, each crop helping the other two. The Haudenosaunee and other peoples called them the Three Sisters, and the partnership is a classic piece of farming wisdom known as companion planting.

The sisters are corn, beans and squash, hilled together into one mound instead of separate rows, so that the plants could shelter and feed one another.

The squash sprawls low between the mounds, and its broad leaves and stems bristle with stiff, prickly hairs that scratch the soft noses of deer and raccoons and keep them out. The same leaves shade the ground, smothering weeds and holding in moisture like a living mulch.

The tall corn gives the beans a pole to climb toward the light, and the beans repay it: their twining vines grip the stalks and brace them like living guy-ropes, so the top-heavy corn does not blow over in a storm.

Corn is a greedy feeder that wears out plain soil within a few seasons, but in the mound the beans refill it: as legumes, they carry bacteria in little nodules on their roots that pull nitrogen from the air and turn it into fertilizer the corn can use.

the-tomatos-slow-road-to-italy.context_blurb:
Few foods seem more Italian than the tomato, sliced on bruschetta, spread on pizza, simmered into sauce, yet no Roman emperor ever tasted one. It took a long, slow road to the Italian table: born in the Americas, it crossed the Atlantic on Spanish ships in the 1500s, then spent generations in Italy as a garden curiosity, feared and admired but not eaten, before it became the red heart of Italian cooking.

The tomato is a New World plant: its wild ancestor grew in the Andes of western South America, and people first tamed it in central Mexico, where the Aztecs were already growing many kinds when the Spanish arrived. After Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec capital in 1521, Spanish ships carried it to Europe, so Italy first saw it only in the sixteenth century.

Even the name comes from the Aztecs of Mexico: their language, Nahuatl, called the fruit tomatl, which the Spanish wrote down as tomate and English later borrowed as tomato. In Nahuatl, tomatl means roughly the plump, swelling fruit.

Italians still call it pomodoro, from pomo d'oro, the golden apple, because the first tomatoes Italians ever saw were little yellow fruits, not red ones; the Sienese naturalist Pietro Andrea Mattioli described the fruit in 1544 as golden when ripe.

Tomatoes were growing in Tuscany by 1548 on the estate of Cosimo de' Medici, but as ornamental plants, admired in the garden rather than eaten, and for more than a century there was hardly a tomato in the Italian kitchen. The reason was fear: the tomato belongs to the nightshade family, kin to deadly belladonna, and herbalists who saw the family resemblance in its small berries assumed it was poison. Across Europe the golden apple picked up a grim new name to match, the poison apple, though only the plant's leaves and stalks are mildly toxic and the fruit itself is safe.

A famous story, disputed by historians and chemists, adds that rich diners who ate tomatoes off pewter plates high in lead really did fall ill, because the fruit's acid leached the lead out, and they blamed the tomato instead of their plates.

The poorer south put it on the plate first: around Naples, then a city ruled by Spain, hungry farmers and cooks began simmering tomatoes into stews and sauces while the wealthier north still held back.

In 1692 Antonio Latini, a chef who ran a household in Naples while Spain ruled the city, printed Italy's earliest known tomato-sauce recipe and called it Spanish-style, alla spagnuola. He meant it as a relish for boiled meats, not for pasta, which had yet to meet the tomato.

Tomato sauce on pasta, the supposed timeless soul of Italian cooking, is only around 200 years old. The first recipes pairing the two appeared around 1790 and in 1837, and the dish spread from the streets of Naples, where vendors ladled cheap tomato sauce over pasta for the poor. The 1837 recipe came from the Neapolitan nobleman Ippolito Cavalcanti, writing in the Neapolitan dialect of ordinary people, and he put his tomatoes over vermicelli.

the-turkeys-transatlantic-name-mix-up.context_blurb:
Every Christmas and Thanksgiving, a bird named after a country in Asia Minor lands on the table, though it never lived anywhere near there. The turkey's name is a pile-up of trading mistakes, and nearly every European language got the bird's home wrong in its own way.

The wild turkey is native to North America, ranging across its south, centre and east, with a second species in Mexico's Yucatán; Indigenous peoples of Mexico had domesticated it by about 800 BC, and the bird never lived wild in Europe, Asia or Africa.

The name belonged first to a different bird, the African guinea fowl: Portuguese traders carried guinea fowl into the Ottoman Empire, England's Turkey merchants bought them there, and the English named the bird after the middlemen's country. When the look-alike American bird arrived in the 1500s, the borrowed name slid across to it and stayed.

Other languages blamed India, because early explorers thought the lands they had reached were the Indies: the French word dinde is a squashed form of poule d'Inde, the hen of India, and in Turkish the bird is hindi. Portugal came closest to the truth, naming the bird peru after the South American region, a real part of the Americas even though the wild bird is North American.

the-tv-dinner-how-the-freezer-left-the-d.context_blurb:
After the Second World War, American freezers made it possible to sell a whole cooked meal frozen in one tray, ready to heat and eat in front of the new family television. The product that launched the idea was born from a Thanksgiving disaster, as the Swanson company tells the story.

In 1953 Swanson over-ordered turkeys and found itself holding 260 tons of frozen birds with nowhere to store them, so it loaded them into ten refrigerated railroad cars and kept the trains moving back and forth across the country, because the cars of that era kept their cargo cold only while the train was rolling.

Rather than throw the turkey away, Swanson turned it into the frozen TV dinner, a heat-and-eat meal that sold about ten million trays in its first full year, 1954, and started a whole industry. The tray idea was borrowed from the airlines: a Swanson salesman, usually named as Gerry Thomas, though the credit is disputed, copied the compartment trays used for in-flight meals, with separate wells for the meat and each side, so the meal went straight into the oven with no dishes to wash.

The hardest problem was safety, and the bacteriologist Betty Cronin solved it: turkey, potatoes and peas had to heat evenly from frozen in one tray, and the turkey was the danger, because as the densest food its centre could stay cold, lingering in the bacteria-friendly danger zone, while its edges looked done.

the-useful-ratios-vinaigrette-3-1-rice-1.context_blurb:
A cook who knows a few simple ratios can make the basics without a recipe. A vinaigrette runs about 3 to 1, oil to vinegar; white rice is about one part rice to two of water. The food writer Michael Ruhlman made the idea famous in his book Ratio: learn the proportion and you can cook any amount from memory.

A vinaigrette uses three times as much oil as vinegar because the oil rounds off the vinegar's sharp bite, so the dressing tastes balanced instead of harsh; straight vinegar on a leaf would make you wince. Three to one is only a launch pad: sturdy, slightly bitter leaves like kale and radicchio can stand a sharper dressing with more acid, about two to one, while tender lettuces want a gentler four to one. The cook Samin Nosrat's advice is to dip a leaf, taste and adjust.

Shaking a vinaigrette breaks the oil into tiny droplets spread through the vinegar, an emulsion, but the mix is temporary: left to stand, the oil and vinegar slowly drift back into separate layers, so a cook gives the jar one more hard shake just before pouring.

Rice works differently from pasta, whose extra water goes down the drain: rice cooks by absorption, and the grains slowly drink up every drop, which is why the water is measured instead of guessed. Once the pot simmers, the lid goes on and the heat goes down low, and trapped steam finishes cooking the grains; lifting the lid to peek lets that steam escape and leaves the rice undercooked or uneven.

Risotto is the rebel: broth goes in hot, one ladleful after another, while the cook keeps stirring, because the stirring rubs starch from the outside of the plump arborio grains, and that loose starch turns the dish creamy, which is also why arborio is never rinsed.

A ratio scales safely where a full recipe may not: double a three-to-one vinaigrette and the proportion simply holds, but double a cake and it can fail, because rising, seasoning and baking time carry chemistry that does not double in step, and a pan twice as wide bakes differently.

the-vertical-spit-shawarma-d-ner-gyro-an.context_blurb:
In Athens it is gyros, in Istanbul döner, in Beirut shawarma and in Mexico City al pastor. The names come from different languages, but all four are the same brilliant piece of cooking: a tall cone of seasoned meat turning slowly beside a fire, its crisp outside carved away as it browns.

Shawarma, döner and gyros are all cooked on a vertical spit, a tall stack of seasoned meat threaded on a rod that stands on end and turns slowly beside the heat. The cook serves it by shaving thin, crisp slices from the browned outer face with a long, flat knife, since only that thin outside layer crisps at once. The meat underneath stays juicy because the spit bastes itself: as the cone turns, fat melts and runs down the stack, keeping the inner layers moist, and cooks even tuck pieces of fat between the layers.

The three names all mean the same thing, turning: döner comes from the Turkish verb dönmek, to turn, Greek gyros means turn, and shawarma comes from a Turkish word for turning. The Greek version, gyros, is usually made with pork or chicken rather than lamb, and it was popular street food in Athens by 1970.

The upright spit was invented in the 1800s in the Ottoman Empire, probably in the city of Bursa; before that, cooks roasted the same seasoned meat threaded on a long spit lying flat above the coals. The name döner kebap does not appear in writing until 1908, but the spit is older than its name: around 1853 to 1855 a British photographer, James Robertson, took what is thought to be the first photograph of one.

Bursa also gave the world the İskender kebab: in 1867, the story goes, İskender Efendi laid thin-sliced döner on soft pide with tomato sauce and yogurt, then at the customer's table poured sizzling butter across it. In 1972 Kadir Nurman, a Turkish guest worker at a stall by West Berlin's Zoo Station, is credited with turning döner into fast food, packing the shaved meat into flatbread with salad and sauce so busy workers could eat on the move.

Lebanese immigrants carried the spit to Mexico around the turn of the twentieth century, and by the 1920s cooks had mostly swapped the lamb for pork; later they crowned the cone with a whole pineapple, whose juice drips down the meat as it turns: tacos al pastor. Mexicans call that spit el trompo, borrowing the word for a child's spinning top.

the-vitamin-hunt-deficiency-diseases-and.context_blurb:
Scurvy, beriberi, goitre and pellagra once killed and crippled people by the million, and each turned out to be caused by something missing from the plate. Tracking each disease to the food that cured it was a long detective story, full of brilliant guesses, stubborn delays and accidental clues.

Scurvy made sailors' gums bleed and old wounds reopen. In 1747 the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind showed, in one of the first controlled trials, that citrus fruit cured it fast. But Lind buried the result in a 400-page book, and the Royal Navy waited until 1795, about 50 years, before giving citrus to every sailor. Lemon juice in the rum ration nearly wiped scurvy out. But in the 1860s Britain switched to cheaper limes from its Caribbean colonies, and scurvy crept back, because a lime carries roughly half as much vitamin C as a lemon. Storing the juice in copper tanks open to the air destroyed still more, and the switch gave British sailors the nickname limeys.

Beriberi, which left people numb and sometimes paralysed, followed polished white rice. The missing nutrient, thiamine, or vitamin B1, sits in the bran and germ, the outer layer and the tiny sprout that polishing scrapes away and throws out. Takaki Kanehiro, a doctor in the Japanese navy in the 1880s, saw that the disease hit ordinary sailors fed on white rice but not officers who ate a mixed diet, so he added meat, vegetables and barley, a grain rich in thiamine, to the ration, and the disease vanished from the fleet. He wrongly thought the extra protein had done it. In the 1890s, in Java, the Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman stumbled on the cause when chickens fed scraps of polished rice developed paralysed legs and recovered on unpolished rice, a clue that later shared in a 1929 Nobel Prize.

Around the Great Lakes, so many people had swollen thyroid glands, goitres, that some army draftees could not button their collars, until doctors began adding iodine to ordinary table salt; Michigan's iodized salt went on sale in 1924, and goitre among its schoolchildren fell from about 39 per cent to under 2.

Pellagra ravaged the corn-eating American South while Mexicans, who ate even more corn, stayed healthy, because Mexican cooks always soaked their corn in lime or wood-ash water, an ancient step called nixtamalization that unlocks the niacin bound inside the kernel; Southern cooks skipped it.

the-wheat-kernel-and-what-milling-remove.context_blurb:
A grain of wheat looks like a single speck, but it has three parts, and what a miller does with them decides whether you get white flour or whole wheat. The story of that choice runs from medieval lords to roller mills to a disease that swept the American South, and it explains why one bag of flour lasts a year and the other spoils.

White and whole-wheat flour can come from the very same field: the brown flecks in whole-wheat flour are flakes of the bran, the kernel's tough outer skin, milled in with everything else, carrying fibre, B vitamins and antioxidants, while white flour is milled from the soft centre alone. A raw wheat kernel is a living seed that sprouts in damp soil, but white flour never will, because the mill threw away the only living part of the kernel, the germ, a tiny speck at one end. The rest of the kernel, the pale starchy endosperm that becomes white flour, is the baby plant's packed lunch, the food it burns to push a root down and a shoot up toward the light.

Almost all of the grain's fibre sits in the bran, the tough brown outer coat that millers sift away, which is why white flour keeps only about a fifth of the whole grain's fibre. The germ is the richest natural source of vitamin E known: a single tablespoon of wheat germ oil holds about a full day's supply, and that vitamin leaves the mill with the germ.

White bread was once a rich man's food in medieval England: a lord's fine white loaf, the manchet, began as the same wheatmeal as his farmhands' dark bread, but servants spent hours shaking the meal by hand through fine sieves called bolting cloths until only white flour was left. Machines made white flour cheap: in 1874 the Hungarian engineer András Mechwart built a mill of paired steel rollers that cracked the kernel open in stages, so the skin sheared away in flakes instead of shattering into the flour, as it did between millstones.

Only about three-quarters of the kernel becomes white flour, and the rest, bran, germ and clinging starch, is sold to farmers as feed for pigs and cattle, so some of the kernel's most nourishing parts go to livestock. White flour keeps for a year while whole-wheat flour turns rancid in months, because milling throws out the kernel's oil-rich parts, the germ above all, and oil is what goes rancid.

In 1837 the Presbyterian minister Sylvester Graham attacked bakers for sifting the bran out of bread and demanded flour from the whole kernel; the bakers ignored him, but his name lives on in graham flour and in the graham cracker, the sweet square sandwiched in a s'more.

White cornbread and molasses left the American South with pellagra, which struck some three million people between 1906 and 1940; after Joseph Goldberger proved it came from diet, millers began adding niacin to flour in the 1940s, and within ten years pellagra had all but vanished. In 1996 American regulators ordered mills to add folic acid as well, to protect babies not yet conceived, and neural-tube defects such as spina bifida soon fell by roughly a thousand cases a year.

Even so, enriched white flour is not the equal of whole wheat, because enrichment puts back only about five nutrients, while milling stripped out dozens, and fibre and vitamin E are never added back at all.

the-zoo-in-your-gut-the-microbiome.context_blurb:
Your colon is home to one of the most crowded communities on Earth: tens of trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome. Far from making you ill, most of them are partners, working on the food you cannot digest yourself and paying their rent in useful chemicals. Counting them, and weighing them, has overturned a few famous numbers.

About 38 trillion bacteria live in the body, nearly all of them packed into the colon, the last stretch of the large intestine, where they finish digesting the leftovers that your own digestion could not break down. For decades textbooks claimed you carried ten bacteria for every human cell, a figure that began as a rough guess in 1972; when Israeli scientists finally counted in 2016, they found about 38 trillion bacteria to some 30 trillion human cells, roughly one of theirs for each one of yours. That careful count also shrank their weight: all your gut microbes together come to only about half a pound, far less than the two or three pounds often claimed.

The bacteria also make nutrients your body makes little or none of itself, vitamins such as K and B12, along with biotin and folate, which are absorbed and put to work. When they ferment the fibre you could not digest, their main waste is a short-chain fatty acid called butyrate, and the cells lining your colon soak it up and burn it as their main fuel, so your own cells literally live on what your bacteria leave behind.

In the American Gut Project, more than 10,000 people sent in stool samples and food diaries, and those with the richest, most varied microbes were the people who ate the greatest range of plant foods, 30 or more different plants a week; the variety mattered more than any diet label.

thiamine-and-beriberi-how-polishing-rice.context_blurb:
Across Asia, polished white rice was long the prestige grain, preferred to plain brown. But in the 1800s, as it became the main food of whole villages, cities and navies, a crippling disease spread with it, and the hunt for its cause gave the world the very idea of a vitamin.

The disease was beriberi: in its wet form it floods the heart and blood vessels, with a racing heart and swollen legs, while dry beriberi attacks the nerves, numbing the hands and feet and buckling the legs. Its cause is a lack of thiamine, vitamin B1, which the body needs to turn food into energy for nerves and muscle, and which rides in the bran and germ, the brown outer layers that polishing buffs away; brown rice keeps it, white rice loses it.

The first clue came by accident. In 1897 in Java, the Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman's chickens fell ill on leftover polished rice from a military hospital and then recovered, because a new cook refused to waste good military rice on civilian chickens and put them back on cheap brown rice. Eijkman realised the sickness came from something missing, not from a germ, and later shared a Nobel Prize.

By 1912 the Polish chemist Casimir Funk named these life-or-death food factors vitamines, fusing vital with amine, a chemical group he believed they all contained; when it turned out that not all of them are amines, the word was shortened to vitamin.

Extracting thiamine from bran gave only tiny amounts, until the American chemist Robert Williams found a way to make it cheaply in 1936, so factories could produce it and mills could add it back into white rice and flour, which is why so many bags now say enriched.

thickening-a-sauce-starch-reduction-gela.context_blurb:
A thin, runny sauce can be thickened in a few classic ways. Most of them add something to the pot: a cook may stir in an egg yolk at the end, or use gelatin, which sets as the sauce cools. One method works the other way, by taking something out, and knowing which is which lets a cook rescue almost any sauce.

Reduction adds nothing at all: the cook leaves the sauce simmering in an open pan, the water escapes as steam, and what stays behind grows thicker and more concentrated in flavour.

The most famous added thickener is a roux, flour and butter stirred over the heat as a paste before the liquid is added, equal parts by weight, so that the fat coats every grain of flour and the sauce thickens smoothly instead of turning lumpy. Three of the five French mother sauces start this way: béchamel loosens the roux with milk, velouté with pale stock and espagnole with brown stock.

three-ways-heat-travels-grill-pan-oven.context_blurb:
A grill, a frying pan and an oven can all be set to the same temperature and still cook a steak three different ways. The reason is that heat can travel in only three ways, by touch, by moving air or liquid, and by invisible rays, and each kind of cooker leans on a different one.

A steak seared in a 400-degree skillet and one baked in a 400-degree oven come out differently, one crusty and one pale, because the heat travels to the meat by a different path in each. A hot skillet works by conduction, heat passing straight from the hot metal into whatever touches it, and that tight metal-to-meat contact gives the hardest, fastest sear.

An oven works mostly by convection: hot air, which physicists count as a fluid along with liquids, swirls around the food and heats it gently and evenly from every side, ideal for roasting and baking but too gentle for a fast sear. A convection oven has a fan that pushes the hot air in circles, evening out the hot top and cool bottom of a still oven and cooking faster, which is why recipes say to set it about 20°C lower.

A grill leans mostly on radiation, invisible infrared rays streaming off the glowing coals through the open air, the same kind of warmth the Sun sends across empty space, which is why you feel a grill's heat before you touch anything. Grill stripes show two kinds of heat on one steak: the dark lines are where the hot bars of the grate touched the meat directly, cooking it by conduction, while the paler gaps between them got only the gentler radiant heat.

toasting-and-blooming-why-you-heat-whole.context_blurb:
Whole spices straight from the jar are sleeping. A good cook wakes them with heat, tipping seeds and pods into a dry pan or a little hot oil for a minute until they darken slightly and the kitchen fills with their smell. That quick step changes what is inside the spice, and when and how you grind it changes it again.

A spice's flavour is stored as tiny droplets of oil sealed inside its cells, aromatic essential oils that stay locked away until heat or grinding breaks the cell walls, which is why a single raw cumin seed smells of almost nothing. The oils are called volatile because they turn to vapour the moment they warm, so a hot pan sends them flying into the air.

Toasting does not just warm up the old flavour; it lightly browns the seed through the Maillard reaction, the chemistry of toast and seared steak, and that browning cooks up brand-new nutty, earthy flavour molecules that the raw seed never had.

Indian cooks often bloom ground spices by frying them in hot oil before any watery ingredient goes in, because most spice flavour molecules dissolve in fat, not in water. The oil soaks up the flavour and carries it through the whole dish, and lab tests have found oil pulling out many times more flavour than water.

Whole peppercorns keep their bite for years, but ground pepper fades within months, because grinding breaks the seed open and spreads its delicate oils across a huge new surface exposed to air, where they evaporate and spoil; cooks buy whole and grind just before using.

Garam masala, the warming spice blend of India, is made by roasting its whole spices, among them cardamom, cloves, cumin and cinnamon, side by side in a hot, dry pan and grinding them only afterwards, so their freshly released oils mingle and marry into one blended flavour that simple mixing cannot give. Chinese five-spice has its own star: star anise, the eight-pointed fruit of an evergreen tree from South China and Vietnam, which is also packed with shikimic acid, the starting material drug-makers use to manufacture the flu medicine Tamiflu.

tofu-cheese-logic-for-the-soybean.context_blurb:
For more than two thousand years Chinese cooks have made tofu, and they make it with a cheesemaker's logic. Dried beans become a creamy milk, the milk is curdled, and the curds are pressed into blocks, and every step has a match in a dairy.

Tofu is made from the soybean: the dried beans are soaked, ground with water and boiled into a white soy milk, a method that goes back to China's Han dynasty. The milk is then curdled with a setter that makes its proteins clump into soft curds and leave watery whey behind, just as a dairy maker curdles cow's milk to make cheese.

One traditional setter is nigari, a bitter, magnesium-rich mineral harvested from the sea: when the ordinary table salt is taken out of sea water and the rest is dried, nigari is what remains.

Warm soy milk slowly in a broad, open pan and a thin, wrinkly skin of protein and oil forms on top, like the skin on hot cocoa; lifted off with chopsticks and dried, it becomes yuba in Japan, a delicacy in its own right.

The difference between silken tofu and firm tofu is pressing: silken and soft tofu is barely pressed or not at all, so it keeps its custard-like softness, while heavy weights squeeze out more of the watery whey to make firm blocks that hold together for cubing and grilling.

Tradition names the inventor as Liu An, a prince of the Han dynasty some 2,000 years ago, whose cooks, or in one telling his alchemists hunting an elixir of immortality, curdled soy milk by accident. Historians call it a legend because no record from Liu An's own lifetime mentions tofu; the story first appears about a thousand years later.
