yogurt-and-cultured-dairy-one-spoonful-s.context_blurb:
Across Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria and India, yogurt has been made the same way for thousands of years: warm a pot of milk, stir in a spoonful saved from the last batch, and leave it somewhere warm overnight. By morning the whole pot has set, thick and tangy. The trick is a colony of living things, and everything about yogurt and its cousins follows from keeping them happy.

Warm milk left alone never becomes yogurt; it just goes bad. That spoonful of live yogurt carries living bacteria, a starter culture, and overnight they multiply through the whole warm pot, souring and setting it; the old method of seeding each batch from the last is called backslopping. The bacteria like warmth close to body heat, roughly 40 to 45°C, held for several hours; much hotter than about 46°C and the living culture dies, while too cold leaves them dormant.

As they feed on lactose, milk's own sugar, the bacteria turn it into lactic acid, which gives yogurt its tart bite. The thickening is the milk's protein, casein, at work: its tiny clusters normally repel one another and keep the milk liquid, but the acid cancels that push, so the clusters lock together into a network that holds the liquid in and sets into a soft gel. The word yogurt came into English from Turkish in the seventeenth century, from a Turkish root linked to condensing and to kneading.

The thin, cloudy liquid that pools on top of a cup of yogurt is whey, the watery part of milk that seeps out of the set curd; it has not spoiled, and many people simply stir it back in. Greek yogurt is ordinary yogurt with one extra step: its watery whey is strained away through cloth, leaving it thick enough to hold a spoon upright, with about twice the protein, and since straining throws liquid away, each cup needs more milk and costs more. The Middle East calls drained yogurt labneh, and Iceland makes skyr.

Kefir, a thin, drinkable cousin, is made with springy, cauliflower-like kefir grains, a rubbery community of bacteria and living yeast, and the yeast gives off a little carbon dioxide, so kefir tingles with a light sparkle that plain yogurt lacks.

Cheese usually sets a different way: instead of waiting hours for acid, the cheesemaker stirs in rennet, an enzyme that shaves the protective strands off the milk's protein bundles so they stick together into curds within minutes.

Yogurt is kinder to many stomachs, too. Plenty of people upset by a glass of milk can eat yogurt made from the same milk, because the bacteria used up much of the lactose as they fermented it, and the bacteria's own lactose-digesting enzymes keep working in the gut.

careme-food-as-architecture.context_blurb:
Marie-Antoine Carême, the great chef of Napoleon's France, taught himself architecture before he became famous as a cook. He worked for the mightiest households of his day, and he crowned their banquet tables with towers of pastry shaped like the world's great buildings. To him, a sweet could be as noble as a cathedral.

His pièces montées, centrepieces several feet tall shaped like Greek temples or Egyptian pyramids, were built from sugar and pastry, with marzipan and nougat, so they were edible, though guests admired them far more than they ate them. One heir of those towers remains the centrepiece at French weddings and christenings: the croquembouche, a tall cone of little cream puffs stuck together with crisp caramel and draped in spun sugar.

Among his savoury dishes he made famous the vol-au-vent, a hollow tower of puff pastry spooned full of chicken and mushrooms in cream, so airy that its name means 'flight in the wind'; he popularised it rather than inventing it, for the name appears in a cookbook of 1739.

He made the tall white toque every chef's badge, scorning the limp caps of the past, and in his kitchens the taller the hat, the higher its wearer ranked; his own stood about 18 inches, stiffened with card. Having fed a Russian tsar, a British prince, the diplomat Talleyrand and the Rothschild family, he earned a famous double title: king of chefs and chef of kings.

He studied architecture from engravings in the national library in Paris and rebuilt temples, pyramids and pagodas in sugar, and he is credited with saying that of the five fine arts, the chief branch of architecture is confectionery.

soul-food-brilliance-from-the-scraps.context_blurb:
Soul food, the cooking of Black Southerners, grew up on plantations where enslavers kept the best meat for themselves and handed enslaved cooks the scraps. Those cooks turned feet, ears, intestines and bitter greens into some of America's best-loved dishes, blending African, Native American and European foods into one kitchen.

The plantation's owners took the hams and roasts for themselves and passed the cooks what they threw away. The cooks scrubbed the hog's discarded intestines by hand and simmered them for hours into chitterlings, often said chitlins, and so little of the pig went to waste that people said they used everything but the squeal.

Watermelon feels as Southern as the Fourth of July, but people first tamed it in northeastern Africa over four thousand years back, and its closest wild relative, the hard, bitter Kordofan melon, still grows in the deserts of Sudan.

Along the Lowcountry coast, the Gullah people created Hoppin' John, black-eyed peas cooked with rice, probably an heir of the rice and beans that sustained captive West Africans during the Atlantic crossing. Families eat it on New Year's Day for luck, the round peas standing for coins, collard greens for folded dollar bills and cornbread for gold.

Collards cooked down for hours alongside a smoked ham hock leave a dark broth that Southern cooks never poured away. They called it pot liquor, or potlikker, and mopped it up with pieces of cornbread, because the greens' vitamins A, C and K and their iron had leached out of the leaves into that broth, so saving it reclaimed the nourishment.

The cornbread itself was a Native American gift: Native Americans first farmed corn, taming a tough wild grass thousands of years ago, and the crop reached Africa and Europe only after explorers carried it out of the Americas. Soul food is a true fusion of African okra, black-eyed peas and rice, Native American corn and the plantation's cast-off European pork, all remade by enslaved cooks.
